Most early Greeks did not even consider 1 to be a number, so they could not consider it to be a prime. By the Middle Ages and Renaissance many mathematicians included 1 as the first prime number. In the mid-18th century Christian Goldbach listed 1 as the first prime in his famous correspondence with Leonhard Euler -- who did not agree. Some mathematicians, including Euler, did not agree about whether 1 is prime, or about the existence of prime numbers. But most today agree with Goldbach and Euler. So it might be considered to be the first or second, or perhaps the third, (who is the first?) or even the fourth prime. But it is certainly not the last.

text: Most species are hermaphrodites—a single animal can produce both eggs and sperm, meaning it can fertilize its own egg, not needing a mate. Others are dioecious—which means male and female species are separate. For most species to reproduce, they need to find a mate. If animals can’t find mates, reproduction isn’t possible. This is why some species are endangered. For example, the population of some species is very low, making it difficult to find a mate. In other instances, a species is vulnerable to predators, or the environment is not friendly for animal life. If conditions are not suitable, animals can have a hard time raising their young. In other instances, environmental conditions cause species to go into extinction. When animal species go extinct, the environment can become unbalanced. Scientists believe the greatest threat facing animals is habitat loss.

Thank God this wasn't based on a true story, because what a story it is. Populated by despicable characters whose depravity knows no bounds, Before The Devil is a mesmerizing, jaw-dropping excursion into perversion which would be laughable (and sometimes is, even with - or perhaps because of - the sickeningly tragic undercurrent of human dysfunction throughout) if it weren't carried out with such magnificent, overwhelming conviction by its stars. The excellent script by Kelly Masterson and superb direction by none other than Sidney Lumet doesn't hurt either.

The main dysfunction here is of a family nature, with the two majorly screwed up brothers (brilliant portrayals from Philip Seymour Hoffman and Ethan Hawke) deciding to rob their own parents' jewelry store, an attempt that goes pathetically awry.

The story is told with time-shifts (which are noted on screen, such as: ""Charlie: Two Days Before The Robbery"", so no one should be confused); some people have said they didn't like this device but I thought it worked perfectly, adding to the skeweredness of the whole affair, considering that the two brothers in question are hardly playing with full decks - between them you couldn't make a decent poker hand to save your life. Of the two the younger brother (Hawke) seems to be the one with the most on his mind, but you can only be so sure because of the way he reacts to everything around him - it's a rather brilliant, albeit sad, performance. The other one (Hoffman) is more down to earth, though not necessarily because he's a more likable person - it's just that the older brother's insanity tends to get in the way; this guy simply seems more grounded, not so much out of necessity but because it's his choice if that makes any sense. These are two amazing, heart-wrenching performances in which you can see the desperation each guy is trying to hide as they embark on their respective journeys to hell - hell being anything but a pleasant place to be. text:
The immune system protects organisms from infection with layered defenses of increasing specificity. In simple terms, physical barriers prevent pathogens such as bacteria and viruses from entering the organism. If a pathogen breaches these barriers, the innate immune system provides an immediate, but non-specific response. Subsequent to this, the specific adaptive immune system provides increased and more specific defenses. The specificities of immune reactions are determined by recognition of major histocompatibility, a molecule located on cell surfaces. As a simple but fundamental example, the MHC molecules on the surface of vertebrates are responsible for recognizing foreign molecules from microorganisms that enter via the gastrointestinal tract or lungs . As MHC molecules bind to bacterial peptides and present the peptides to CD8 T cells, these T cells kill foreign cells. MHC molecules also present molecules derived from viruses to CD4 T cells that can also kill infected cells . In contrast, self peptides derived from vertebrate cells are presented to CD4 T cells that inhibits killing of self cells, resulting in tolerance to the self . The ability of the immune system to provide specific protection to self is an important mechanism for survival during embryonic and fetal development. The MHC proteins are generally encoded by chromosome 6 of the human genome.

Their most distinctive feature is the ‘combs’ – groups of cilia which they use for swimming – they are the largest animals that swim by means of cilia. Adults of various species range from a few millimeters to 1.5 m (4 ft 11 in) in size. Comb jellies are usually translucent and pulsating with bright pink, yellow or orange areas.
The phylum comprises five classified families in three recognized genera. Species of these families in the genera Cestum, Cestopelma and Cestopsis (which is more closely related to Cestum) are commonly called ctenophora. The largest family, Cestida, comprises one genus whose members are more commonly called “comb jellies” or “comb jellies and salps” in the United States and “salp” in the United Kingdom. Cestidae and Cestoplanidae are the other two families.
The only species in this phylum previously known to science was Pleurobrachia bachei, a marine species discovered off Santa Barbara, California, United States, in 1983 by Dr. Ronald Greeley (University California). The Computer Science Network (CSNET) was a computer network funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF) that began operation in 1981. Its purpose was to extend networking benefits, for computer science departments at academic and research institutions that could not be directly connected to ARPANET, due to funding or authorization limitations. It played a significant role in spreading awareness of, and access to, national networking and was a major milestone on the path to development of the global Internet.
The Computer Science Network (CSNET) is a research and educational computer network, supported by the Computer and Information Science and Engineering Directorate of the United States National Science Foundation. Its purpose is to extend the benefits of networking to all of the Departments of Computer Science in Universities and Research Colleges which are not directly connected to the Arpanet.
In the 1970s, the National Science Foundation (NSF) awarded a portion of their ARPANET connectivity grant (the first grant given in 1974) to the University of California at Berkeley. That institution immediately became a member of the Arpanet, with NSF awarding additional grants to many other universities and research institutions.
In late 1981, the Director of NSF's Computer Research Program Division created a CSNET Working Group led by John Butler of the University of Connecticut. The purpose of this group was to determine if a non-ARPANET, nationally-scoped network of Internet gateways could be constructed, with NSF providing only the minimal funding required, to accomplish this task.

One of the claimants of the English throne opposing William the Conqueror, Edgar Atheling, eventually fled to Scotland. King Malcolm III of Scotland married Edgar's sister Margaret, and came into opposition to William who had already disputed Scotland's southern borders. William invaded Scotland in 1072, riding as far as Abernethy where he met up with his fleet of ships. Malcolm and Edgar were joined by their cousins, King David of Scotland and Llewellyn of North Wales and Wales. Malcolm III was a grandson of King Cernach, while David I of Scotland was a grandson of King Kenneth III and great-grandson of King Donald II, making the kings descended from both Donald and Cernach, giving each king his legal claim to the Scottish throne. Malcolm III was made king by his vassal, King Owen of Strathclyde.

Unfortunately, even many with formal computer science training have a weak understanding of the concept.So here's a simple and concise explanation:P vs. NP The P vs. NP problem asks whether every problem whose solution can be quickly verified by a computer can also be quickly solved by a computer. (Wikipedia)So let's figure out what we mean by P and NP.P problems are easily solved by computers, and NP problems are not easily solvable, but if you present a potential solution it's easy to verify whether it's correct or not.As you can see from the diagram above, all P problems are NP problems. If you've run a program to solve a problem, you don't need to check every time whether the solution is correct! The following example shows a very interesting situation: you have an NP problem and can't easily compute the solution so you run a program to solve it. Now, if the program is correct, it will verify the solution (and give one, if it exists). Thus, it will be easier to solve NP problems than to find the solution. (Wikipedia)So let's look at some example scenarios:Scenario 1: You need a short time to solve an NP problem.Scenario 2: In this case, you have a short but indefinite amount of time. In other terms: you can spend a lot of time to solve the problem, but sometimes you can solve it in little time. If you're able to do that (meaning: if you can solve the problem in little time) than you will be able to solve NP problems faster

From previous observation, one could see that two combustible materials would produce more heat and light than one combustible material alone. This made scientists wonder if the extra heat was produced by an invisible substance. This invisible substance was called fire or phlogiston. Fire was believed to be a pure substance that burned in the presence of oxygen. In phlogiston theory, the product of combustion was believed to be a form of phlogiston that was believed to be an invisible substance.

Sheffield City Region (SCR) signed a deal in 2015 paving the way for a mayor with certain devolved powers. Former chancellor George Osborne, who signed the deal, had previously said elected mayors were key to devolution.
But Sir Steve said the city region’s approach is very much “local, independent and determined”.
He said: “We’re very, very different to [Greater] Manchester: what we’re doing isn’t a mayor, we’re doing an authority.
“From a financial point of view the mayor is not necessary. So we’re not going to be doing that.
“If you come to Sheffield, what we’re doing is an authority in a local government structure – that’s the difference.”
SCR will have four devolved powers, in health, education, transport and housing.

text: The final major evolution of the steam engine design was the use of steam turbines starting in the late part of the 19th century. Steam turbines are generally more efficient than reciprocating piston type steam engines (for outputs above several hundred horsepower), have fewer moving parts, and provide rotary power directly instead of through a connecting rod system or similar means. Steam turbines virtually replaced reciprocating engines in electricity generating stations early in the 20th century, where their efficiency, higher speed appropriate to generator service, and smooth rotation were advantages. They were also used on many ships for similar reasons, but these are less numerous than stationary electricity generation applications. Steam turbine power plants are generally much larger than reciprocating engine plants. Because of the turbine's ability to produce consistent high rpm, it is also important at low speeds for many marine applications. This was especially true for naval ships, but many small merchant vessels also retained turbine engines for this reason. Today, large commercial ships and larger merchant vessels usually have diesel engines as their primary power source, while smaller commercial vessels almost always use diesel engines as well. Meticulously constructed and perfectly played, To The Ends Of The Earth is a simply astonishing voyage out of our reality and into another age.

Based on William Golding's trilogy, these three 90-minute films chronicle the journey towards both Australia and experience of youthful aristocrat Edmund Talbot (Benedict Cumberbatch) aboard an aging man o' war in the early 19th century as he heads for a Government position Down Under.

Among the crew and hopeful emigrants sharing his passage are a tempestuous, bullying captain (Jared Harris), a politically radical philosopher (Sam Neill), a canny 1st lieutenant who's worked his way up from the bottom (Jamie Sives) and, fleetingly, the first brush of love in the form of a beautiful young woman (Joanne Page) whose ship literally passes in the night.

Quite aside from the astonishing degree of physical historic accuracy, director David Attwood and screenwriters Tony Basgallop and Leigh Jackson have a canny eye and ear for the manners and stiff etiquette of an earlier time, crafting a totally convincing microcosm of the Napoleonic era.

Shipboard life is one brutal, monotonous round of seasickness, squalor and danger after another and as Edmund becomes entangled in the loves, hopes and miseries of his fellow passengers he experiences a delirious whirl of life's hardships, Man's inhumanities and his noblest sentiments.

Those who enjoyed Master And Commander: The Far Side Of The World or Patrick O'Brian's series of novels on which it was based will love this  for everyone else, it's a whole new world to discover." text: From the Eocene onwards, the ongoing Alpine orogeny caused a N–S rift system to develop in this zone. The main elements of this rift are the Upper Rhine Graben, in southwest Germany and eastern France and the Lower Rhine Embayment, in northwest Germany and the southeastern Netherlands. By the time of the Miocene, a river system had developed in the Upper Rhine Graben, that continued northward and is considered the first Rhine river. In the latest Miocene, the Rhine river began to cut a steep valley into the Lower Rhine Embayment. The Rhine’s direction of flow was changed several times in its journey to the North Sea. By the early Upper Miocene, the river’s course was altered once more, towards the Main (Rhine-Klasse). In order to get there, the river had to cross the Haarberg mountain range. From there onwards, the northern Rhine valley ran roughly straight northwards. In the Middle Miocene, the river’s course was altered and it took a westerly direction to cross the Rhine graben, towards the northwest. The geological history in the Rhine and Main river valleys shows that they were formed at the same time. The river flow is still being determined by the Upper Mos- and Kanz-Graben. (Wikipedia)

Connection-oriented transmission requires a setup phase in each involved node before any packet is transferred to establish the parameters of communication. Ethernet is an example of a network with connection-oriented transmission.

Exposure to a O 2 partial pressures greater than 160 kPa (about 1.6 atm) may lead to convulsions (normally fatal for divers). There is the possibility that chronic high-oxygen exposure may eventually lead to pulmonary disease in air-breathing divers such as scuba divers or surface-supplied divers. In the 1940s, when deep diving and compressed air oxygen systems were first introduced into the United States Navy, an epidemic of "diver's lung" occurred in divers breathing 100% air. This problem was solved by the use of 20% oxygen and 80% nitrogen breathing mixtures. Since that time, 3% to 10% oxygen breathing mixtures have been used by military and recreational divers to safely conduct deep air diving, without chronic respiratory problems. This is an art film that was either made in 1969 or 1972 (the National Film Preservation Foundation says 1969 and IMDb says 1972). Regardless of the exact date, the film definitely appears to be very indicative of this general time period--with some camera-work and pop art stylings that are pure late 60s-early 70s.

The film consists of three simple images that are distorted using different weird camera tricks. These distorted images are accompanied by music and there is absolutely no dialog or plot of any sort. I was completely enthralled by this film--perhaps because it was exactly what I was in the mood for on this particular day. But I was also really excited about the movie because it seemed like a very well-executed abstract film that challenged conventional notions of storytelling, while retaining some visual appeal.

In the end, the movie left me a little puzzled. It was definitely a weird film, but I couldn't quite figure out where it was going. Did it have a deeper meaning, a hidden narrative, or was it really only about distorting images?

Anyway, it was a really cool movie that I'd watch again, and I definitely think some people will find it very thought provoking as well. But, please, know what you're getting into when you put this DVD in!!

In 1872, the Central Pacific Railroad established a station near Easterby's—by now a hugely productive wheat farm—for its new Southern Pacific line. Soon there was a store around the station and the store grew the town of Fresno Station, later called Fresno. Many Millerton residents, drawn by the convenience of the railroad and worried about flooding, moved to the new community. Many Fresno residents, by contrast, moved to the less conveniently located railroad communities in the foothills, such as the town of Bard, later renamed Bard.
In 1882, the railroads began constructing dikes and embankments to protect against the floods. This resulted in a large drainage area: Today, most of the drainage flows north through the Fresno River and a diversion tunnel under the Sierra. Many dams have been constructed in the Fresno or San Joaquin valleys since the first dikes were built. The railroad eventually gave up on Fresno Station as a station stop for passengers—after an extended stop for dinner, passengers disembarked. And the railroads reorganized. The Central Pacific absorbed the Western Pacific Railroad and the Southern Pacific absorbed the Central Pacific in 1885.

The service started on 1 September 1993 based on the idea from the then chief executive officer, Sam Chisholm and Rupert Murdoch, of converting the company business strategy to an entirely fee-based concept. Sky One also later formed part of the subscription fee.
The same satellite transponder was used for the analogue subscription service and the subscription-free Sky Digital service, meaning the analogue service was not an original part of the Sky Digital platform and required its own additional equipment to receive it on a regular satellite receiver. This also meant that there were some receivers that could not receive the analogue service due to band-width limitations.
The analogue service originally had a different encryption scheme to the digital service, the older analogue encryption scheme was removed as soon as Sky Digital became available. This led to some analogue service receivers gaining a larger range of service without additional hardware. In some cases, the receiver will accept a signal in the same way that a digital converter box will receive the encrypted digital signal.

text: In Japan, at the end of the Asuka period (538–710) and the early Nara period (710–794), the men who fulfilled roles similar to those of modern pharmacists were highly respected. The place of pharmacists in society was expressly defined in the Taihō Code (701) and re-stated in the Yōrō Code (718). Ranked positions in the pre-Heian Imperial court were established; and this organizational structure remained largely intact until the Meiji Restoration (1868). It was during the Heian period (794 –1192) that we first see the use of the title, pharmacy, and drug names associated with it (Figure 2). Interestingly, some members of the aristocracy of the Imperial court were named after drugs and botanical or insect species as a form of prestige. Moreover, in the Heian period, we begin to see an increase in the use of written text for drug names and their indications. These written texts also provided information such as dosage, safety and use of specific drugs in the treatment of various diseases. In 905 we see the Heian government officially established a pharmaceutical office. In 929 we see the establishment of the Japanese government and this organization established a pharmaceutical office where pharmacy officials were named (Figure 2). Through these activities of the pre-Meiji government, we also see the rise of the pharmaceutical industry, the rise of the pharmacist as a professional and an increase in the pharmaceutical sciences. All four schools were based on the same intellectual foundation, but advocated different theoretical approaches toward medicine. The four schools were the School of the Yellow Emperor, the School of the Nanjings, the Wujing "five pure" school, and the Huangji "six extraordinary" school. The Wujing and Huangji schools were formed respectively around 1120 and during the reign of Hongwu in Ming period (1368–1396). Zhu Dikun and Wang Shizhen, two prominent physicians of the Ming period, both advocated "six extraordinary" theory based on the Huangji school of thought. Yin Shanshen (1674–1747) wrote a commentary titled Yin Shanshen Huangji Jijing on the sixth chapter of the Huangji Jijing written in 1120. Yin wrote his commentary in 35 chapters, in which he further analyzed the Huangji Jijing. Chapter 1 described the theory behind the "six extraordinary" (i.e., six special organs with special functions), whereas Chapter 2 described special functional organs in each zang-fu organ system. Here is a very simple example:class NotifiedAction implements ActionInterface { private $action; public function __construct(ActionInterface $action) { $this->action = $action; } public function notifyUser() { // Logic for user notification } public function trigger() { $performed = $this->action->trigger(); $this->notifyUser(); return $performed; } }As you can see, we now have a NotifiedAction class that implements the same interface and that takes the same interface as a constructor parameter. Note that this class inherits from the ActionInterface class and that it implements all the required methods from there. What we are doing here is that we are implementing all our functionality in a class that has a simple construct method and the implement method.Note that we also add the notifyUser method here. This is where we do our actual magic. Then we delegate all the information to the ActionInterface class and call it back, so that it executes the default trigger method of the Interface. In PHP 5.4 (with PSR2 compatibility), you can create a trait (using a naming convention) and make these rules as PHP sees them. Necrotising stricture of the oesophagus presents as a painful, indolent and often lethal tumour. It is rarely encountered by the surgeon, but when it is diagnosed, aggressive surgical management is crucial to the patient's survival. The aetiology is usually unknown, but there may be genetic causes. Necrotising esophageal stricture is more likely to develop in the elderly, and most common sites of involvement are between the 3-4th and 11-12th oesophageal vertebrae. In the Western world, it most commonly occurs in men, and is frequently misdiagnosed or managed by gastroenterologists, resulting in a late diagnosis. When in contact with a magnet, there is an excess force due to the magnetic interaction of neighboring molecules that tends to squeeze the liquid O 2 into a thin film against the surface of the magnet [3]. This behavior is used in magnetometers, the measurement instruments that use O 2 to measure the magnetic field and that are used in fields such as geological exploration to locate oil and mineral deposits. text: A construction project is a complex net of contracts and other legal obligations, each of which all parties must carefully consider. A contract is the exchange of a set of obligations between two or more parties, but it is not so simple a matter as trying to get the other side to agree to as much as possible in exchange for as little as possible. The time element in construction means that a delay costs money, and in cases of bottlenecks, the delay can be extremely expensive. Delay can also be expensive in that it can ruin a company's reputation and lead to costly injuries to its workers and to a potentially devastating liability claim. Because of the importance of delay in the performance time and schedule of construction projects, the parties to a construction contract have an obvious incentive to try to delay performance as much as possible to delay payment or to increase the cost of the project to the owner, while the owner has to try to limit delay to limit cost overruns. This article focuses on the ways that parties can try to avoid delays in construction, the problems which can create delays, and finally the legal rights which a party can have to avoid a delay causing legal liability. A construction project often consists of dozens of separate contracts, each of which with different parties and each of which in which one party is a general contractor for the other party. text: The customary law of Normandy was developed between the 10th and 13th centuries and survives today through the legal systems of Jersey and Guernsey in the Channel Islands. The system consisted of the jury, the customary laws of the villages, and the Norman law. Under this last, the civil law was determined by the customary laws of each village, while the criminal law was the same everywhere. Accordingly, under the law of Normandy, there was no distinction between civil and criminal law. The jury law of each village, or parrocch, was known as the "droit parracca". The parracca, or parrai (plural), were the ancient Normans before the Norman conquest, who were later called the "Cuisses de bois" (wooden legs) but it was known that if a man was a descendant of a noble family, he might be able to sit on judgment. The Normans thereafter adopted the growing feudal doctrines of the rest of France, and worked them into a functional hierarchical system in both Normandy and in England. This was due to the fact that feudalism made better sense on an island than on the mainland of France. At the time that William was beginning to expand his power across Normandy, it had not yet spread to the south of France, allowing him to expand uncontested at the fringes of feudalism. This last point is in response to skeptics who argued that, given the lack of flea transfer, plague must have spread directly from human to human—by a different agent, at a different time. A house that provides less utility to a millionaire as a summer home than it would to a homeless family of five, is an example of reduced "distributive efficiency" within society, that decreases marginal utility of wealth and thus the sum total of personal utility. An additional dollar spent by a poor person will go to things providing a great deal of utility to that person, such as basic necessities like food, water, and healthcare; while, an additional dollar spent by a much richer person will very likely go to luxury items providing relatively less utility to that person.
This does not mean, however, that we are therefore forced to have economic equality for all – a principle that has many problems and which is considered to be the same position (no inequality) as its polar opposite (unequal). Rather, economic equality for all is merely a principle that should be used in designing our society when designing a society is beneficial or necessary. It has not been proven to have any benefits that make it worth using instead of any of its negatives (positive and negative), but that doesn't mean it is necessarily bad to use. However, both suspects must confront each other, as Fonda is in love with Stanwyck, but she has become obsessed with Fonda's best friend. And yes, you read that right - it's a best friend triangle!

The best part of the film has to be Barbara Stanwyck. She makes the film worth watching alone. Lake Constance consists of three bodies of water: the Obersee ("upper lake"), the Untersee ("lower lake"), and a connecting stretch of the Rhine, called the Seerhein ("Lake Rhine"). The lake is situated in Germany, Switzerland and Austria near the Alps. It also consists of the city of Konstanz, Germany and the Swiss towns of Kreuzlingen, Mehringen, and Kemme, near the Austrian border. Apart from the town of Konstanz, the lake consists entirely of protected natural areas. The lake is divided into smaller bodies of water by several peninsulas. One of these islands, called Kreuzlingen Island, contains a natural reserve with a diverse plant species. The islands of Sommerschwanden and Eigersberg, situated near Eggersfeld, are not part of the lake because their surfaces are too large. Lake Constance is the third largest lake in Germany, after Chiemsee and Balsersee. The largest island, the one with the name Mehrings, is used as a camping ground and contains two of the most popular beaches of the lake. The town of Kreuzingen sits close by Mehrings Island.

"Lake Constance" redirects here. For other uses, see Lake Constance (disambiguation).

text: due to the recent cases of _ algorithmic bias _ in data - driven decision - making , machine learning methods are being put under the microscope in order to understand the root cause of these biases and how to correct them . here  , we consider a basic algorithmic task that is central in machine learning : subsampling from a large data set . subsamples are used both as an end - goal in data summarization ( where fairness could either be a legal , political or moral requirement ) and to train algorithms ( where biases in the samples are often a source of bias in the resulting model ) . in the absence of any specific or explicit bias in the training data , the resulting statistical model ( and associated feature selection methods ) is often non - discriminatory . but in the presence of bias ( for example gender stereotyping ) then the features selected are likely to be biased too . to understand how these subsampling techniques impact algorithmic bias , we study the behavior of the subsampling procedures ( for example stratified subsampling ) on a range of statistical models - including linear regression , logistic regression and deep neural net architectures - on a range of biased ( gender stereotyping ) and non - biased ( age and income ) features. on this small scale ( 2 data sets , 2 feature sets ) , it is not clear if the models are producing statistical discrimination or just statistical bias. with this limited number of data and feature sets , we are unable to reach definitive conclusions about the performance of the models either in terms of bias versus discrimination , or whether gender stereotyping is contributing to the model or not. but the model training methods ( the sample subsampling methods ) are contributing to the bias - or simply to statistical variance - not the statistical models themselves. we conclude that sample subsampling methods are a source of algorithmic - and therefore possibly - legal - bias in machine learning methods.

The analysis identifies the major drivers of the results from open-economy models and compares estimates from four major studies that have examined corporate tax incidence in an open economy. The studies vary in the assumptions of critical elasticities, and the variations account for differences in the reported estimates. The estimates from the four studies range from 0-30 percent. The results indicate that a greater share of the corporate tax burden on consumers is associated with free trade. This result implies that reducing trade barriers would lessen the burden on households from the corporate tax. Trade liberalization would also benefit domestic U.S. manufacturers that compete both domestically and in global markets as well as the U.S. consumers who would incur less of a tax burden. In particular, this open economy literature indicates that trade liberalization will reduce the burden on U.S. consumers from the corporate tax.This paper was prepared for presentation at a conference sponsored by the Federal Reserve Bank of Boston and the Federal Reserve Bank of New York on "The Economic and Fiscal Implications of the Tax Incentive Proposals in the Bush Plan." I am grateful to an anonymous referee for very thoughtful comments that encouraged the author to make a significant revision. I also wish to thank Richard Peck, the Director of Research and Analysis of the Fiscal Policy Center, in Washington, D.C., for providing some helpful comments on my earlier draft. When H O exists in solution, it rapidly undergoes chemical decomposition to form ( H O or ) oxides or ( H O or ) hydroxides. Thus the living creatures or the water itself removes the excess of H P and therefore prevents the oxygen from either being completely decomposed away or oxidized to an oxygen-free carbon dioxide. Microorganisms or toxins that successfully enter an organism encounter the cells and mechanisms of the innate immune system.
When foreign substances or toxins enter the bloodstream, specialized cells are dispatched to identify the threats. The innate immune system is comprised of two branches: the first of which includes phagocytic cells. The phagocytic cells form a specialized branch of phagocytic cells called the macrophages that actively engulf and destroy foreign substances, particularly bacteria, by ingesting them. This process occurs all the time in the body, the most common form of which is during the clearance of dead cells and tissues. The cells are not really specialized, but they are well-known for their ability to identify and attack foreign substances.
The other branch of the innate immune system is the pattern recognition receptors or PRRs. PRRs are specialized cell-surface receptors that identify pathogens by recognizing specific structures or sequences of a foreign substance. PRRs respond to pathogens by signaling the immune system to trigger and initiate the immune response. The most commonly known PRRs are the TLRs, but there are also PRRs that target bacteria, viruses, or nucleic acids.

Areas of polar glaciation. Map by CCA Graphic
During glacial periods, atmospheric water vapour concentration is greatly reduced (as happens today on Antarctic icebergs). Since icebergs release some of this water vapour when melted, global cooling is not inevitable even at such high latitudes.
But during glacial interglacial periods, such as at present, atmospheric water vapour concentration (inferred from atmospheric oxygen isotope concentrations) increases and global cooling becomes almost inevitable.
In other words, icebergs release both atmospheric water and oxygen into the air. The icebergs of Antarctica and Greenland alone add more atmospheric water to the air than all of the rainforests on Earth put together. So their influence on atmospheric moisture is immense.

Starting in the late 1950s, American computer scientist Paul Baran developed the concept Distributed Adaptive Message Block Switching with the goal to provide a fault-tolerant, efficient routing method for telecommunication messages as part of a research program at the RAND Corporation, funded by the US Department of Defense. This concept contrasted and contradicted the theretofore established principles of pre-allocation of network bandwidth, largely fortified by the development of telecommunications in the Bell System. This development resulted in 1972 in a patent for the Distributed Message Block Switching with two co-inventors.

The idea of the Adaptive Message Block Switching was subsequently implemented in practice by a number of telecommunications companies. Deutsche Telekom implemented the technique for ATM (Asynchronous Transfer Mode), Deutsche Telekom AG v. PT/IP Holdings LLC, 468 F.3d 1253 (Fed. Cir. 2006). US Federal Circuit Court of Appeals upheld patent infringement by the competitor PT/IP Holdings LLC. Deutsche Telekom's ATM product was named "ADMIS". ATM was an "unpatented and generally known industry practice" according to the "Federal Circuit", and therefore infringed the "ADMIS" patent.

The steam engine contributed much to the development of thermodynamic theory; however, the only applications of scientific theory that influenced the steam engine were the original concepts of harnessing the power of steam and atmospheric pressure and knowledge of properties of heat and steam. The experimental measurements made by Watt on a model steam engine led to the development of the separate condenser. Watt independently discovered latent heat, which was confirmed by the original discoverer Joseph Black, who also advised Watt on experimental procedures. In his letters to Black, Watt also stated that he had "examined" the theory of Black. Since in 1782 Watt became familiar with the theory, it appears that he understood the theory of latent heat and possibly had a general understanding of the theory of thermal expansion. Since these theories contributed greatly to the development of thermodynamics, they should be studied thoroughly. In this paper, we will focus on Watt and discuss several topics that we believe will contribute to a better understanding of his career. We will first review the contribution of the steam engine, the separate condenser and other components of the system, the experiments by Watt, his knowledge of the theory, and his understanding of thermodynamics. In order to make a better understanding of his achievements, we will also compare our findings with the results of the previous research.

The evolutionary strategy used by cicadas of the genus Magicicada make use of prime numbers. These insects spend most of their lives as grubs underground. They only pupate and then emerge from their burrows after 7, 13 or 17 years, at which point they fly about, breed, and then die after a few weeks at most. This is a strategy which is shared with some other species such as the mayflies and the fireflies, that uses also the prime numbers, but their interval of expression is shorter. This strategy, by contrast, has no biological advantage: there is actually less of a disadvantage of emerging less frequently than other species who emerge just once in their lives. The evolutionary strategy used by the cicada is only a consequence of the fact that we live in a society where people use computers with an average of 4 and 10 digits in the numbers they use. So, in Pubblico Ministero v Ratti because the Italian government had failed to implement a Directive 73/173/EEC on packaging and labelling solvents by the deadline, it was estopped from enforcing a conflicting national law from 1963 against Mr Ratti's solvent and varnish business. A member state could "not rely, as against individuals, on its own failure to perform the obligations which the Directive entails."
The Court also held a Directive may provide member states with "a general principle," an idea which, if adopted, would "be binding" on states. There are some exceptions: e.g., Directive 89/662/EEC on driving licences, which provides an obligation for a state to require the issue of a licence to a holder of a full driver's licence in another Member State, does not create horizontal direct effect because "[E]xcusing itself from the obligation would not seriously impair the effectiveness of the Directive." The Court's understanding appears consistent with Professor Dicey's view that a statute cannot bind a state to do anything; it can only provide information: A state which acts in a manner contrary to the statute is subject to challenge in the courts. It may be that the Court's view on this point has in the last ten to twenty years been somewhat diluted: although not formally changed, the Court appears to have begun acting as a rule-making body for the European Union where one would never have expected such a role a generation ago. This is nearly impossible to do, even for an adept meditator.3) Letting imaginative experience play through our awareness with no emotional or ego driven interference. This is again very difficult to do with any degree of success. But it is the key to becoming our best selves. Now the next thing to note on the left is that we are here working with the imagination and therefore the intellect. In this talk we present a variant of the standard model (SM) which describes the gauge symmetry group under two mass scales $M_R$ and $M_L$ to which all SM particles below the cutoff are assumed to unify. Under this set up two distinct gauge symmetries govern the low energy physics with the exception of gravity, the first (a ``small'' group) being broken at the scale $M_1$, while the second one (a ``large'' group) at the scale $M_2$, and thus there exists a non-trivial composite sector carrying the broken gauge symmetry. We investigate a simple variant of this setup, namely where the ``small'' and ``large'' groups are nonisomorphic gauge groups.

text: Stage 1 is the first, or introductory stage of the bill, where the minister or member in charge of the bill will formally introduce it to Parliament together with its accompanying documents – Explanatory Notes, a Policy Memorandum setting out the policy underlying the bill, and a Financial Memorandum setting out the costs and savings associated with it. Statements from the Presiding Officer and the member in charge of the bill are also lodged indicating whether the bill is within the legislative competence of the Parliament. Stage 1 usually takes place, initially, in the relevant committee or committees and is then submitted to the whole Parliament for a full debate in the chamber on the general principles of the bill. If the bill is a money bill or one which alters the law of Scotland, a separate Stage 1 will take place and, once again, the debate will focus on the general principles of the bill. A separate Stage 1 may also arise if there are disagreements between the party groups on the text of the bill in the committee stage. A large number of bills usually pass Stage 1 with no major amendments accepted. Stage 2 is the stage when the committee or committees dealing with the bill report their recommendations to the whole Parliament. Amendments can also be accepted or refused at this stage before the final motion is made which, if passed, will enable the bill to proceed to the final stage. The stage is formally brought to an end when the Scottish Rules of Parliament authorise the minister or parliamentary counsellor to proceed with the bill without further formalities. The bill text and relevant documents can then be found on the Parliament s website at Legislation. Parliament.scot. The boiler is a high temperature heat source for a Rankine cycle, while the Brayton cycle includes no boiler, and no thermal power plant, its components and functions are designed to be small and light-weight. The boiler is generally the largest component of a Rankine power cycle and requires a large footprint, so the design of a boiler has tradeoffs between cost of boiler construction and efficiency. With a Brayton cycle, the components are simply designed to have a certain set of properties, and the structure does not have to be optimized between cost and efficiency like the boiler structure of a Rankine cycle does. There is no tradeoff between cost and efficiency in the structure of the Brayton cycle. A particularly simple example of a probabilistic test is the Fermat primality test, which relies on the fact (Fermat's little theorem) that np≡n (mod p) for any n if p is a prime number. The Fermat test is the Probabilistic test mentioned above, but it is not the only one: for example, the Probabilistic Miller-Rabin test is the Probabilistic version of the Miller-Rabin test, which is another widely used Probabilistic algorithm.

In the compound engine, high-pressure steam from the boiler expands in a high-pressure (HP) cylinder and then enters one or more subsequent lower-pressure (LP) cylinders. The complete expansion of the steam now occurs across multiple cylinders and as less expansion now occurs in each cylinder less heat is lost by the steam in each. A high-pressure compound engine could run for several hours without refueling or reloading the boiler. The steam could now be directed to pumps, turbines, and other mechanical devices across an entire factory with a single boiler. Woolf's engine was an enormous improvement over Newcombe's, but it was also large, expensive, and difficult to operate. The fourth Yuan emperor, Buyantu Khan (Ayurbarwada), was a competent emperor. He was the first Yuan emperor to actively support and adopt mainstream Chinese culture after the reign of Kublai, to the discontent of some Mongol elite. He had been mentored by Li Meng, a Confucian academic. Li advised him to give priority to education and administrative reform, and also urged him not to use the traditional Mongol method of dividing the population into four classes and using them as a labor force, thus leading Yuan China to modernization. In 1283, Buyantu was crowned, after that he made a reform in administration, including making a special office of treasury and having Chinese officials to administer the central treasury, in order to limit the use of silver by the officials, and also he issued an edict banning forced labor of peasants, which was important to promote the development of China.

text: Computational complexity theory is a branch of the theory of computation in theoretical computer science that focuses on classifying computational problems according to their inherent difficulty, and relating those classes to each other. A computational problem is understood to be a task that is in principle amenable to being solved by a computer, which is equivalent to stating that the problem may be solved by mechanical application of mathematical steps, such as an algorithm. In other words, computational problems involve procedures that can be effectively implemented, albeit at a cost that can be unacceptably high in practice. There are three aspects to a computational problem: Problem definition: Describe the problem in words. Solve the problem: Devise or use a technique to actually solve the problem. Analysis: Theoretical analysis of computational problems, including, e.g., computational efficiency and efficiency, complexity theory, and parallel and distributed processing. There are four basic classes of computational problems. Solvable Problems: Problems that are completely solvable either by definition, e.g. the factorization problem or by a known algorithm. Unsolvable Problems: Problems that are believed, via computational proof, to be completely unsolvable, e.g. the traveling salesman problem. (A solvable problem that cannot be solved is known as an "undecidable problem.") Complex Problems: Problems that are solvable, but not efficiently nor with a known algorithm. text: In 1993, Galor and Zeira showed that inequality in the presence of credit market imperfections has a long lasting detrimental effect on human capital formation and economic development. Although credit markets have improved substantially over the past 20 years, Galor and Zeira' 993 empirical findings have remained untested since then. This paper provides the first empirical evidence on human capital formation and economic growth in the presence of credit market imperfections. We measure both economic growth and human capital formation by an index of life expectancy at birth and a human capital index constructed by using data from United Nations Development Program (UNDP, 1994). We examine the impact of credit market imperfections on both economic growth and human capital formation. Our data set include 114 countries for the period 1950 to 1990. We use a variety of independent sources to measure credit market imperfections and their impact on economic growth and human capital. We find some evidence that credit market imperfections cause a long lasting increase in human capital formation by about 30 per cent of a decade. However, we find little evidence that credit market imperfections cause an increase in aggregate economic growth by about 5-15 per cent of a decade.

For a precise definition of what it means to solve a problem using a given amount of time and space, a computational model such as the deterministic Turing machine is used. The time required by a deterministic Turing machine M on input x is the total number of state transitions, or steps, the machine makes before it halts and outputs the answer ("yes" or "no").
The machine uses 1 symbol of memory at any time; hence the "Turing machine" has no memory and just uses that, hence the "deterministic" part. The machine may not repeat the same operation; it must make some fresh change of state at each step. The machine must be able to mark the tape at some locations, and is allowed to mark the tape at any location in the process of answering "yes" to the question x. The space that machine uses is the total of the areas of the locations on the tape where it puts marks. The machine may mark more than one location at a time, but must eventually put back into the past every location on the tape marked, and leave each location blank. For this model, the "time" is the running time of the machine.
The time measure is used as a metaphor for the time between when someone first becomes aware of the problem and when she or he has decided what, if anything, to do about it. In fact, when the person first starts thinking of the problem and may be unaware that she or he has the problem, time is not considered to be passing at all. It's only when the person decides that the problem is interesting in some way and wants to think about it further that time is considered to be passing. The "space" used by a Turing machine is measured as the number of locations that have ever been marked during the execution of the machine.

We review the role of squeezing and symmetry breaking in some theories of vacuum instability. A simple two-level model of coupled spin polarizations in vacuum is discussed. We then analyze a more complex model involving two coupled polarizations, whose dynamics depends on parameters of the quantum noises associated with squeezing and decoherence. The instability of the two-polarization model is related to a bifurcation condition in a coupling between the polarizations, caused by decoherence. We analyze a model in which squeezing is replaced by symmetry breaking. As a result, the phase space of the polarizations collapses in the direction transverse to the symmetry axis. Symmetry breaking occurs in a critical system even if the intrinsic parameters remain below the instability threshold. Symmetry breaking and squeezing are both effective in generating instabilities for polarization states. A general model of coupled polarizations is considered in which both symmetry breaking and squeezing occur. The model shows the transition from self-sustained motion to the decay of incoherent polarizations. Symmetry breaking is shown to suppress the decay of the polarizations. text:
Evolution of the adaptive immune system occurred in an ancestor of the jawed vertebrates. Many of the classical molecules of the adaptive immune system (e.g., immunoglobulins and T cell receptors) exist only in jawed vertebrates. However, a distinct lymphocyte-derived molecule has been discovered in primitive jawless vertebrates, such as the lamprey and hagfish. This lymphocyte-derived molecule, known as a V(D)J recombination product, is distinct from the classical adaptive immune system molecules because it is highly expressed in embryos and is also present in nonjawed invertebrates. Furthermore, V(D)J recombination products are highly conserved in bony fishes, which, despite possessing a highly evolved adaptive immune system, retain a low level of expression. V(D)J recombination products and antigen-presenting molecules do not exist in nonjawed invertebrates; the latter exist only in the primitive and jawed vertebrates and are absent in some classes of nonjawed invertebrates, such as the arthropods and mollusks. Collectively, this data suggests that the adaptive immune system evolved prior to the diversification of jawed vertebrates. Furthermore, the highly conserved presence of V(D)J recombination products and antigen-presenting molecules in bony fishes strongly suggests that the adaptive immune system evolved independent of the more complex hagfish, lamprey, and jawed vertebrate adaptive immune system.

Such qualifications were introduced under the House of Commons Disqualification Act 1975 and the British Nationality Act 1981. Specifically, members must be over the age of 18 and must be a citizen of the United Kingdom, the Republic of Ireland, one of the countries in the Commonwealth of Nations, a citizen of a British overseas territory, or a European Union citizen resident in the UK.
Members are disqualified from being elected if they are in the Service of the Crown, either by payment or by pension.

text: The mirror image of ghost particlesThe GERDA experiment supplies no new evidence that neutrinos are their own antiparticlesNeutrinos are the most elusive particles having extremely weak interactions with all other particles. They have rather unusual properties and are even expected to be identical with their own antiparticles. So far this property is, however, not experimentally verified. In 2004 a group of scientists called GERDA from the Federal Institute for Research of Engineering in Mainz started to build a new detector to make it possible to verify the mirror symmetry between ghost particles and antighost particles or to verify that neutrinos are their own antiparticles.The experiment is based on a detecting method of ghost particles. These ghost particles come from the decay of radioactive isotopes of xenon, an element that normally is not radioactive. The xenon atoms are enclosed in a crystal detector. When ghost particles decay they emit photons, called scintillation photons in this case. These photons stimulate photons emitted from material components of the crystal, such as zinc oxide or potassium iodide. These photons are then detected by a light detector. The photon energy is measured by a calorimeter. The detector is located about 20 meters underground in the Germanys GERDA (Germany) experiment, located at the LKP (Laboratory for Particle Physics) in Mainz.After one month of data taking, GERDA has not detected any particle oscillation or mirror symmetry violation. text: The mechanisms used to evade the adaptive immune system are more complicated. The simplest approach is to rapidly change non-essential epitopes (amino acids and/or sugars) on the surface of the pathogen, while keeping essential epitopes concealed. This is called antigenic variation. Antigenic variation involves both the generation of a new antigen and the prevention of antibody binding. This approach can sometimes be used to elude a single antibody (called monovalent). Multiple antibodies (called polyvalent) can still bind the pathogen, which can be fatal after repeated exposure. Polyvalent antibodies also have the ability to opsonize bacteria for phagocytic cells. This is a major benefit for infectious organisms. In order to evade recognition by multiple antibodies, another mechanism must occur. This involves the rapid turnover (synthesis and degradation) of many surface antigens at different sites on the pathogen surface . This process is called antigenic oscillation. Antigenic oscillation is also beneficial after repeated exposure. Pathogenic bacteria such as Yersinia often undergo this process and are able to avoid reactive immune systems for longer time periods . Antigen specificity allows for the generation of responses that are tailored to specific pathogens or pathogen-infected cells. Furthermore, sleep disruption can lead to decreases in cognitive functioning, as well as reductions in our immune response that can result in higher infection rates. Finally, when we are suffering from a decrease in sleep, our circadian rhythm can be negatively impacted as well, as sleep deprivation can actually delay the rhythm by a few hours. By understanding the connections between light and our sleep cycles, as well as how sleep deprivation can affect the immune system and our circadian rhythm, we can be better equipped to address issues that arise from decreased, distrupted, or reduced levels of sleep. In this same period, William Wordsworth’s poem “The World Weary” (1804)—in which, in the voice of an aging woman, he wonders what use there is in getting out to battle again (though she does not use the specific term ‘battle'), and reflects on a life, in the end, with nothing much to show for it—inspired a contemporary writer and revolutionary, the Irish patriot John Philpot Curran, to deliver a well-known and often quoted oratorical denunciation of violence.

This series, made for Televisión Española (TVE) is basically a series of chapters in the life of an ordinary family in 1968, primarily as seen through the eyes of the youngest son.

Based on a background of historical events, such as the May 1968 student uprising in France, the decaying Franco regime, the war in Viet-Nam, the rise of imperialism, and others specifically related to Spanish life at that particular moment, one might regard this series as a simple compilation of characteristic foibles which make themselves so apparent in this kind of entertainment.

Generally treated in a lightweight vein though not lacking in certain moments which might be called dramatic, the series would seem to be aimed at people of around fifty who can rember those times, as, it should be stated, anyone younger either chooses to ignore such happenings or is busily occupied in other things.

The best thing that can be said of this series is Ana Duato's rôle as mother of three children: she plays the part of the total housewife of the times really well, manifesting that peculiar Spanish penchant, especially noticeable among women, of letting all her thinking and her doings be carried forward by the impetus of her heart, without any resorting to the use of the brain. As we say in Spain, common sense is one of the least common senses. She seems an ideal housewife of that kind -- one always sees her around the house -- while she is just not quite so ideal on her way to the supermarkets

Though there are episodes which might be called historical in which the characters take part in events of some consequence, they are mostly of the type that could have taken place anywhere in the world, and at a time when the world was not divided into countries, and before the wars broke out and divided the world into countries against each other. The whole series might be described as a series of anecdotes, rather than true to life events, though not absolutely false, and all in all rather fun, sometimes serious and sometimes humurous, but above all light as one can not imagine.

Despite their soft, gelatinous bodies, fossils thought to represent ctenophores, apparently with no tentacles but many more comb-rows than modern forms, have been found in lagerstätten as far back as the early Cambrian, about 515 million years ago. There is also a long-standing tradition of theorizing that ctenophores are closely related to cnidarians (another large phylum whose representatives include sea anemones and jellyfish); evidence for this suggestion includes morphological similarities and genetics. However, this hypothesis remains controversial; studies on this subject are not free of conflict, and many of them are inconclusive. More than anything, this suggests that we know relatively little about these organisms.
Detailed morphological and molecular studies now indicate that the ctenophores form a distinct clade of bilaterian animals that is more closely related to crustaceans and cnidarians than it is to vertebrates and mollusks. They are placed at the base of the class EuARthropoda.

Natural killer cells, or NK cells, are a component of the innate immune system which does not directly attack invading microbes. Rather, NK cells destroy compromised host cells, such as tumor cells or virus-infected cells, recognizing such cells by a condition known as "missing self." This term describes cells with low levels of a cell-surface marker called MHC I (major histocompatibility complex) – a situation that can arise in viral infections of host cells. If the "missing self" condition is detected before a compromised host cell undergoes further changes (which would be signaled by increased levels of MHC I) it is usually destroyed by NK cells. text: To further highlight the difference between a problem and an instance, consider the following instance of the decision version of the traveling salesman problem: Is there a route of at most 2000 kilometres passing through all of Germany's 15 largest cities? The quantitative answer to this particular problem instance is of little use for solving other instances of the problem, such as asking for a round trip through all sites in Milan whose total length is at most 10 km. The problem instance itself does neither exhibit any special qualities, nor the general characteristics, which are required to solve traveling salesman types of problems. Consequently, the 2000 kilometres instance is not even particularly interesting. A better (real world) example of a traveling salesman problem instance would be an instance for a route passing through all of the United States's 50 states with a total length of at most 4000 km. Is there a route passing through 50 states with at most 4000 km which does not travel along the same route? This is an algorithmic question, which can be answered by means of dynamic programming. text:
Tainted look at kibbutz life

This film is less a cultural story about a boy's life in a kibbutz, but the deliberate demonization of kibbutz life in general. I was hoping for a little historical insight, but all I got was an agenda-filled piece of filmmaking that tries to fit all the negatives of life in a kibbutz into 40 minutes of the film.

The filmmakers don't ask why things happen on the kibbutz, they just assume they happen and that they are to blame. The narrator is extremely condescending. It's like they think the audience is idiots that need to be spoon-fed what's right and what's wrong. As if a kibbutz is bad simply because it is a kibbutz. As if life on the kibbutz can't be good because it is a kibbutz. As if the life on the kibbutz is worthless just because it is a kibbutz.

The role of committees is stronger in the Scottish Parliament than in other parliamentary systems, partly as a means of strengthening the role of backbenchers in their scrutiny of the government and partly to compensate for the fact that there is no revising chamber. The principal role of committees in the Scottish Parliament is to take evidence from witnesses, conduct inquiries and scrutinise legislation. There are also two internal committees of the Parliament, which is an unusual feature of the Scottish Parliament. The two internal committees, which are not mentioned elsewhere in this document, are the Scottish Parliamentary Corporate Body ( SPCB) and the Public Petitions Committee ( PPC). The SPCB is the managing body of the Parliament, and the PPC is the main committee dealing with petitions. The committee system Although the Scottish Parliament is a relatively new body, the committee system is not unprecedented. In 1998 the First Minister launched a process to reform committee structures, and to enhance the capacity of committees. This action only made matters worse in the eyes of the Chinese, who then thought that the Mongols were the ones who deserved this punishment. text: In addition to identifying rocks in the field, petrologists identify rock samples in the laboratory. Two of the primary methods for identifying rocks in the laboratory are through optical microscopy and by using an electron microprobe. In an optical mineralogy analysis, thin sections of rock samples are analyzed through a petrographic microscope, where the minerals can be identified through their different properties in plane-polarized and cross-polarized light, including their birefringence, pleochroism, twinning, and interference properties with a conoscopic lens. An image of the rock section can then be imaged to record the mineral composition of the thin section. An electron probe analysis is used to identify the composition of individual minerals (including their chemical composition) within a thin section. This analytical method is similar to an electron microprobe analysis because it uses an electron probe to bombard a sample of the rock at a high energy. However, the electron probe sample is less powerful than a primary electron beam and is more accurately used to analyze individual mineral phases within a rock. Both of these methods can provide useful information about the mineralogy of the rock, including the type of rock, the composition of the rock sample, the grain size of individual minerals, and the distribution of individual minerals. However, they cannot provide information at the scale of individual grains (millimeter to sub centimeter) within a rock. In 1943, geochemist Frank H. Kruber determined that an electron probe could be used to determine the composition of the individual mineral phases (including their chemical composition) within a rock. However, many of the earlier instruments for chemical analysis of rocks were unable to resolve the individual crystals of the minerals within a rock and to identify their chemical composition. The ability to determine the chemical composition of a mineral was limited because of the difficulties involved with analyzing a small-sized sample in the electron microscope. In some countries, private schools have better educational outcomes than public schools. Although this is usually due to higher quality teachers in the private schools, it is possible that the quality of public schools is decreasing faster than private schools are improving. This would suggest that private schools would serve as a check on the educational performance of public schools, and this possibility should be studied empirically. Private schools can be more selective than public schools and, as a result, typically have higher education outcomes. This is especially so if private schools are paid a fixed fee, as is common in many countries. In this arrangement, with limited capacity, private schools can and will select the most able applicants, those most likely to get the most from the education provided. In such a system, there are two benefits from having private schools. First, private schools offer a quality education to the best applicants. Second, by being more selective in enrolling students, private schools provide additional educational opportunities, especially for those with low skills. Shrewsbury in 1970, who noted that the reported rates of mortality in rural areas during the 14th-century pandemic were inconsistent with the modern bubonic plague, leading him to conclude that contemporary accounts were exaggerations. The plague theory remained the orthodox interpretation for 400 years, until Walter Reineke’s study in 1992 used scientific techniques to replicate medieval plague epidemics under controlled field conditions. Reineke’s work replicated the plague of 1351, a severe outbreak caused by viral infections, without killing large portions of the population. Reineke’s work also replicated medieval plague outbreaks caused by bacterial infections. Using archaeological techniques and the historical record, he established that the medieval plagues could only be bacterial infections, not viral. Moreover, his work showed that the infections caused an average of 15% out of the population to die, whereas the Black Death caused more than one-half to die. However, the plague theory continued to persist as scientifically valid after Reineke’s study. Lobates have eight comb-rows, originating at the aboral pole and usually not extending beyond the body to the lobes; in species with (four) auricles, the cilia edging the auricles are extensions of cilia in four of the comb rows. In the lobe rows, four (and possibly five or six) comb-rows are present; usually the lower three comb-rows contain cilia and the upper three (and perhaps a fourth) have (sometimes, as in Phoba sp.) simple oral pistons. Some Lobatinae (Phoba) show a "double locker" type of arrangement with a series of cilia beginning at the aboral pole, followed by a series of comb- rows with cilia, then cilia and (potentially) comb rows. Most lobe rows are (or may be) unciliated.
The larvae of the Lobatinae are distinguished by the reticule organs, which in most species consist of three lobes originating from the ventral surface beneath or behind the mouth. Each lobe has a stalk and branches out into a mesh of cilia. These cilia are used to gather food. The food is directed to the mouth by the cilia and digested by a pair of grapnel organs that resemble the tails and legs of a crayfish.
The cilia of the reticule are oriented vertically so that the reticule is constantly agitating like a net, pulling in its prey (microorganisms) as it moves. The question of whether P equals NP is one of the most important open questions in theoretical computer science because of the wide implications of a solution. If the answer is yes, many important problems can be shown to have more efficient solutions. These include various types of integer programming problems in operations research, many problems in logistics, protein structure prediction in biology, and the ability to find formal proofs of pure mathematics theorems. However, if the answer is no, then this will have the important implication that the ability to prove the existence of NP-complete problems will also give a proof of the existence of unsolvable problems. Moreover, because algorithms in NP will be easy to design and use, it will be difficult to verify them, making possible cheaters. Harvard's athletic rivalry with Yale is intense in every sport in which they meet, coming to a climax each fall in the annual football meeting, which dates back to 1875 and is usually called simply "The Game". While Harvard's football team is no longer one of the country's best as it often was a century ago during football's early days (it won the Rose Bowl in 1920), both it and Yale have influenced the way the game is played. In 1903, Harvard Stadium introduced a new era into football with the first-ever permanent reinforced concrete stadium of its kind in the country. It is believed to have been the inspiration for the construction of the University of Michigan's legendary Michigan Stadium in 1927. In recent years, Yale and Harvard have been the schools most frequently represented on the nation's most prestigious and most-coveted All America teams. Each fall, Harvard's football meets that of Yale, the most significant contest of Harvard's season. Each student body, as it has since the early days of the game, attempts to outdo that of its rival in spirit, intensity, enthusiasm and noise for the Yale contest. This long tradition continues to exist even as the attendance rates are dropping in the modern age of television. The tradition of spirit in athletic competition, the fact that Harvard and Yale students and alumni "outdo" each other in spirit and intensity, is the longest running and most successful intercollegiate athletic rivalry. The fact that Harvard and Yale meet three times each season and that the outcome of their meetings affect the national champion is also extremely unique.

[note 3] The spelling with Rh- in English Rhine as well as in German Rhein and French Rhin is due to the influence of Greek orthography, while the vocalisation -i- is due to the Proto-Germanic adoption of the Gaulish name as *Rīnaz, via Old Frankish giving Old English Rín, Old High German Rīn, Dutch Rijn (formerly also spelled Rhijn)). The diphthong in modern German Rhein (also adopted in Romansh Rein, Rain) is a Central German development of the early modern period, the Alemannic name Rī(n) retaining the older vocalism,[note 4] as does Ripuarian Rhing, while Palatine has diphthongized Rhei, Rhoi. The German-spelt name is also retained in French Rhin.[4] The spelling with the diphthong, -ie-, is also used in Dutch, German and Romanian Rhein. English, Dutch, German, Danish, Norwegian and Swedish have adopted the older form, with the spelling of English and Dutch as Rhine, Dutch Rijn, German Rhein, Danish Ryn, Norwegian Rjån and Swedish Rhei. English and Dutch are also used to transliterate Greek Ῥήν (Rhīn). The other spelling with -i-, -Rhin-, occurs in French and Italian river names and names of places (such as in Italy), as in English as well. Many such engines have been designed, from the time of James Watt to the present day, but relatively few were actually built and even fewer went into quantity production; see link at bottom of article for more details. The major problem is the difficulty of sealing the rotors to make them steam-tight in the face of wear and thermal expansion; the resulting leakage made them very inefficient. A modern example is the PSE-220 power station (2.15 MW net) in Tainan, Taiwan, which uses a "tangential" version of the Wankel engine. There are relatively few applications for a mechanical Wankel engine in the steam world; the exception being a small generator attached under the boiler of a steam locomotive, so that its diesel could be run without disturbing full time operation of the locomotive. An engine of similar construction to that of a steam locomotive could be set up to run parallel to a reciprocating steam engine with a conventional piston and cylinder arrangement, to drive the same boiler through the steam connection and feed pump, thus providing a small amount of extra power. members unanimously approved eliminating a "sunset clause" from the oversized vehicle ordinance based on positive feedback from residents, community leaders and the Police Department.They say the law's positive impact on safety, aesthetics and parking availability trumps the hassles it has created for some local recreational vehicle owners who have had to begin paying for storage lots or using their yards.City officials estimate there are roughly 100,000 recreational vehicle owners in San Diego.Some community leaders have also expressed concerns that the ordinance has increased homelessness by forcing some people who had been sleeping in RVs onto the streets.The law, which would have expired in August without the council's vote to eliminate the sunset clause, primarily targets tourists with large campers who sleep inside their vehicles to avoid paying for hotels or other accommodations, particularly during summer months.This practice often means trash on the street, loitering outside the campers and other problems that turn some neighborhoods into makeshift campgrounds.The law also cracks down on people who use city streets to park their boats, non-motorized vehicles and other large vehicles.The law prohibits such vehicles from parking on any San Diego city street or in any public parking lot between 2 a.m. and 6 a.m., and makes it illegal to park those vehicles within 50 feet of any intersection at any time of the day.An oversized vehicle is defined as one more than 27 feet long and more than 7 feet tall.The law includes exemptions for school buses, some city vehicles and commercial vehicles making deliveries.The city has posted more than 300 red-and-white signs throughout San Diego explaining the new law, mostly near freeway exits.Residents say the problem became steadily worse in San Diego before the law was passed in August 2014, partly because most other cities along the coast had previously adopted similar bans.San Diego spent more than seven years crafting the new law, with the largest sticking point being whether it should apply citywide or only along the coast.Pacific Beach residents Lou Cumming praised the city for making the law permanent, predicting the problems would revive without it. "These visual eyesores present safety hazards and health hazards and they reduce the quality of life in our residential neighborhoods," Cumming said.Other residents say they support the law, but complained that police need to step up enforcement.Some also say it's forced them to begin contacting city code compliance officers, because many RV owners are now illegally parking them in side and front yards.Lt. text: The simplest valve gears give events of fixed length during the engine cycle and often make the engine rotate in only one direction. Most however have a reversing mechanism which additionally can provide means for saving steam as speed and momentum are gained by gradually "shortening the cutoff" or rather, shortening the admission event; this in turn proportionately lengthens the expansion period. However, as one and the same valve usually controls both steam flows, a short cutoff at admission adversely affects the exhaust and compression periods which should ideally always be kept fairly constant; if the exhaust event is too brief, the totality of the exhaust steam cannot evacuate the cylinder, choking it and giving excessive compression ("kick back"). So, in order to have constant, optimum speed for the conditions, the admission cutoff must be proportionately lengthened and so reversal is only done when and where truly expedient. In steam locomotives, the exhaust cutoff is also subject to a reversing effect when the excess steaming causes the exhaust valve to shut slightly later than the intake cutoff. This in turn lengthens the exhaust and compression periods and increases speed even further. But now, the exhaust is not completely expelled as the valve closes and thus the intake is also affected in a diminishing manner, to the point that it even cuts off ahead of the intake cutoff. Hence when the exhaust valve finally shuts (at low speed, the admission cutoff is often set to the point of closure), the excess steam continues to flow into the cylinder and so an excessive piston speed arises, which is detrimental to the engine. If the exhaust cutoff is then reversed, the engine can move faster again. An alternative valve gear which can overcome these disadvantages is the "wagon" or "rocker" valve gear. Here the reversing of the valve is not controlled by a simple spring mechanism, but rather there is an auxiliary mechanism which can change the position of the valves under steam pressure.
