EU Competition law has its origins in the European Coal and Steel Community (ECSC) agreement between France, Italy, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg and Germany in 1951 following the second World War. The agreement aimed to prevent Germany from re-establishing dominance in the production of coal and steel as members felt that its dominance had contributed to the outbreak of the war. Article 65 of the agreement banned cartels and article 66 made provisions for concentrations, or mergers, and the abuse of a dominant position by companies. The ECSC agreement is notable for its use of EU law on competition policy, rather than national legislation. However, this created tensions with other EU law areas, most notably with the free movement of persons, which is an overarching principle in EU law. An examination of the tensions between competition law and other aspects of EU law is important for the purpose of this paper, with specific reference to free movement of goods, services and capital. The tension in EU jurisprudence between a vision of EU law as a unified legal system and an emphasis on legal heterogeneity in the treaty itself (now exacerbated by the Lisbon treaty) is one aspect of the EU legal system that has received little academic attention. This paper attempts to address the gap by examining the EU law-making process in the area of social policy. Drawing on legal typology, this paper argues that EU law in this area follows a three-stage model of legal integration. The stage model and the legal typology in its use provide a novel method of examining EU law to the benefit of EU legal theory. This paper employs quantitative legal comparative techniques to uncover the tensions in the EU legal system from a comparative empirical perspective. text: Under the Scotland Act 1998, ordinary general elections for the Scottish Parliament are held on the first Thursday in May every four years (1999, 2003, 2007 and so on). The date of the poll may be varied by up to one month either way by the Monarch on the proposal of the Presiding Officer. If the Parliament itself resolves that it should be dissolved (with at least two-thirds of the Members voting in favour), or if the Parliament fails to nominate one of its members to be First Minister within 28 days of a General Election or of the position becoming vacant, the Presiding Officer proposes a date for an extraordinary general election and the Parliament is dissolved by the Queen by royal proclamation. If a general election is held on another date, the Parliament is dissolved before the election has taken place. Parliamentary constituencies are unnamed electoral divisions and, unlike constituencies at Westminster, have no official names or boundaries but are defined only by numbers. The Scottish Parliament (either prior to 2007 or at a subsequent time) has the power to determine which areas should constitute parliamentary constituencies and to prescribe their numbers and boundaries. It may make new constituencies and it may alter the boundaries and numbers of existing constituencies. Prior to May 2007, the Parliament could alter constituencies only after an order laid before it by the Presiding Officer and notified to the Secretary of State for Constitutional Affairs. After 1 May 2007, constitutional changes made by the Supreme Court of the United Kingdom and the Scottish Parliament require the approval of both the Scottish Parliament - and by virtue of the Scotland Act 1998 the Westminster Parliament. An example of IBM's 3033 data communications interface, the second of Baran's two patent applications (1964)

Although an electronic switch for switching traffic, Baran's packet switch was integrated with his network interface into its terminal end of a network line connecting computers or other devices. I find this somewhat surprising, as this film is not great (or even good), but neither is it terrible (or even really bad). What this film really is, is...depressing. Because "I, Robot""s depressingness is, in the end, not so much about robots or about AI. It is, instead, more of a metaphor for the death of an era, and the birth of a lesser and unimaginative one. And that, to me, is a sad state of affairs.

In this film, the near-future has become a kind of backwater of an age where things have changed radically--but in ways that the average "I, Robot"" viewer probably doesn't understand all that clearly. This film depicts a near-future where robots are everywhere. But they aren't doing anything. They are just standing around--looking a bit like robots. They also have that familiar "robot" expression--you know, the one where a computerized and soulless human being somehow seems alive and almost (but not actually) human. These are the kinds of robot-people that one might imagine a child from 100 years a future would describe to his or her parents (if not actually "living" humans), as being so lifelike that they have "wings," they have "feet," and they can "dance and sing." But they can't really do any of those things. They are, in effect robots--people who look a bit (but not really) like a person. And they can't do any of the things that a human being can do. They are just standing around.

text: Some theories developed in the 1970s established possible avenues through which inequality may have a positive effect on economic development. According to a 1955 review, savings by the wealthy, if these increase with inequality, were thought to offset reduced consumer demand. A 2013 report on Nigeria suggests that growth has risen with increased income inequality. In the 2010s, there is a view that high inequality may help stimulate economic growth in poorer developing countries, where the poor compete more for a limited number of "opportunity jobs". According to the theory, the competition between the rich and the poor forces businesses to create more jobs and increase productivity to provide higher wages; the jobs are filled mainly by the poor. According to this view, increasing prosperity and reducing poverty are driven by competitive markets; government regulation is harmful, and government intervention to change the distribution of wealth, or to raise the income of the poor, is counterproductive. However, there are questions as to whether competition among the poor actually leads to better job opportunities. The theory has been challenged, both economically and philosophically. The views are seen as inconsistent with some basic tenets of economics, as well as contrary to evidence from the real world. Economists have found that increased inequality can retard growth, and reduce employment and wages for the poor; the poor spend more than the wealthy, so any reduction in spending by those in the upper income groups acts as a drag on economic growth. In addition, increases in consumption rates by the upper income groups lead both to increased consumption of goods and services made or provided by the poor: the demand for the goods or services created by the poor leads them to hire more people or buy more equipment; consequently, those living in income groups 2 to 4 (lower middle class) see their consumption rise and their unemployment rate drop

text: Construction projects can suffer from preventable financial problems. Underbids happen when builders ask for too little money to complete the project. Cash flow problems exist when the present amount of funding cannot cover the current costs for labour and materials, and because they are a matter of having sufficient funds at a specific time, can arise even when the overall total is enough. Projects can also come to an end because of poor management, misuse of funds or unethical practice. The World Bank conducted a global survey of construction projects in 2011 and 2012 . They identified that between 10% and 40% of all-in project costs were lost to mismanagement, fraud, corruption and poorly defined scope. For large projects , it was between 13% and 49% . Mismanagement is the most likely cause of overrun on projects and it is the greatest risk factor associated with project cost increases - it should therefore be avoided. Economist Joseph Stiglitz argues that rather than explaining concentrations of wealth and income, market forces should serve as a brake on such concentration, which may better be explained by the non-market force known as "rent-seeking". While the market will bid up compensation for rare and desired skills to reward wealth creation, greater productivity, etc., it will also prevent successful entrepreneurs from earning excess profits by fostering competition to cut prices, profits and large compensation. Stiglitz argues that the former market influence is greater than the latter market influence. However, in the long term, it has been observed that competition in the financial system has led to excess profit-making, which has been shown to lead to rent-seeking and other market distortions.
Laissez-faire advocates also note that capital has a habit of overcoming labour. When capitalism reaches its limits, technology will eliminate much of the remaining economic inequality. For example, most of the economic benefits accruing to top 1% in the USA have come from the increase in productivity of American workers since the middle of the 20th century. These gains are due to the rise of capital equipment, automation, and improvements in physical capital. This is a result of the industrial revolution, which has benefited both capital and labor. However, as technologies continue to grow in importance for wealth creation, it will be possible for workers and their capital to continue to prosper.
In its purest form, laissez-faire capitalism requires no governmental regulation at all. Supporters argue that the government should regulate only when the private sector fails to do so. Free movement of goods within the European Union is achieved by a customs union, and the principle of non-discrimination. The EU manages imports from non-member states, duties between member states are prohibited, and imports circulate freely. In addition under the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union article 34, ‘Quantitative restrictions on imports and all measures having equivalent effect shall be prohibited between Member States’.
The customs union is a significant barrier to trade, but once goods cross the union’s external border they are free to circulate throughout Europe and may be taxed in their country of final destination. A non-taxable goods flow within Europe is known as the common trade of goods (CTG) of the free market. In practice, a number of national fiscal regimes operate in parallel and tax CTG accordingly.
The concept of a common external tariff which would form the fourth pillar of the CTM was rejected by the French in the Single European Act 1986, as the proposed duty structure would allow Germany to export a surplus of manufacturing goods to France, whilst France would be allowed to import luxury goods free of duty from the UK. The French feared this would create a permanent net loss of manufactured goods, and a perpetual trade balance deficit.
The common trade of goods requires a means to collect the duties which, in the absence of a common corporation tax, must usually be collected from the importer. If an importer has not paid any corporation tax they are treated as a non-trading entity. EU Directive 2006/112/EC sets out the conditions which must apply before import duty rates can be raised above the common trade of goods. text: James Hutton is often viewed as the first modern geologist. In 1785 he presented a paper entitled Theory of the Earth to the Royal Society of Edinburgh. In his paper, he explained his theory that the Earth must be much older than had previously been supposed in order to allow enough time for mountains to be eroded and for sediments to form new rocks at the bottom of the sea, which in turn were raised up to become dry land. He suggested that the Earth had passed by in three or less intervals. His theories were largely met with acceptance by Sir Robert. Hutton’s publication of the Theory of the Earth became an important geological text and remains so today. The book was eventually published in 1795 and became a major contribution to early modern geological theories. Hutton also wrote a second book entitled Observations on the Volcano of 1795. Both books explored the ideas of continental drifting and of a cycle of the Earth’s existence. Hutton developed the idea that the continental movement was caused either directly or indirectly by the Earth’s internal heat, which made it likely that the movement may have reversed direction as the inner heat changed. Steven Barkan writes that if defendants plead not guilty, "they must decide whether their primary goal will be to win an acquittal and avoid imprisonment or a fine, or to use the proceedings as a forum to inform the jury and the public of the political circumstances surrounding the case and their reasons for breaking the law via civil disobedience." A technical defense may enhance the chances for acquittal but make for more boring proceedings and reduced press coverage. During the Vietnam War era, the Chicago Eight used a political defense, while Benjamin Spock used a technical defense. The Chicago Eight case was more public because it involved well-known activists, whereas the case of Dr. Baird was technical and involved fewer people. While the legal battles for a number of cases are ongoing, the information that defendants in the Baird case are not being held in contempt for nonpayment of fine is helpful in understanding the differences between the 1960s and the 1990s and the differences between civil disobedience and protest.

The nine scholars analyzing Japan's economic crisis from 1985 through 2000 have identified six underlying causes:Surplus in Savings: Japan has traditionally enjoyed an unusually high savings rate and a comparatively low consumption rate. During the decades of recovery and high-speed growth, this "savings surplus" supplied sorely needed capital to private industry in the form of bank loans. When the banking system collapses, the surplus is drained and is no longer available. Surplus in Labor: Since 1954, the Japanese government has maintained a labor surplus that has consistently added to Japanese GDP (see Figure 1). In short, the demand for labor was always less than the supply, which is a unique situation in the world of economics. text:
The Rankine cycle is the fundamental thermodynamic underpinning of the steam engine. The cycle is an arrangement of components as is typically used for simple power production, and utilizes the phase change of water (boiling water producing steam, condensing exhaust steam, producing liquid water)) to provide a practical heat/power conversion system. The heat is supplied externally to a closed loop with some of the heat added being converted to work and the waste heat being removed in a condenser. The Rankine cycle exists in a number of different configurations and can be used for both electrical power generation and process heating and cooling applications. An understanding of the fundamental physics and thermodynamics associated with the steam power cycle can be beneficial in the development of alternative energy conversion devices, the improvement of the thermodynamic performance of conventional steam power plants and the design of process heating/cooling equipment. This paper presents an introductory overview of the Rantine cycle and its application in the context of conventional and renewable energy power conversion and process heating/cooling applications

Some well known problems that are classified as hard include prime factorization, the integer factorization conjecture, and the discrete logarithm problem. 1979's Tourist Trap is a clever, unique B thriller that stands out as one of the best of it's kind.

Travellers stop at a lonely wax museum where the owner's mannequins are a little too life-like for comfort.

While the film has hints of The Texas Chainsaw Massacre, Tourist Trap is mainly a creepy psychological thriller worthy of The Twilight Zone. Director David Schmoeller gives this movie an atmosphere of darkness and mystery, that reaches nightmarish proportions. Also, Schmoelloer adds the occasional touch of comic relief to the bizarre happenings.

Venteran actor Chuck Connors is the best of the film's decent cast. His role as an ex-cop who now runs the wax museum as a tourist trap is one of his better performances.

Tourist Trap is a unique thriller from beginning to end that is deserving of a DVD release.

text: When B cells and T cells are activated and begin to replicate, some of their offspring become long-lived memory cells. (See Figure 9.) I've written about it, preached about it, taught Coming of Age classes about it, and been pulled into countless coffee-hour conversations with newcomers. Everyone in America seems to know that religious organizations exist to promote some set of beliefs that their members share. But they don't seem to know that a religious organization such as the UUA is supposed to promote something different--the values and aspirations of the membership. In fact, the mission statement of the UUA has the value of equipping people to live their faith, not promoting a set of beliefs.It may surprise readers to know that my interest in the subject dates back to high school. While I was taking classes at the Unitarian Universalist Congregation at Shelter Rock, the New York Unitarian Church hosted a visit by UUA President Clark Upton. I remember being fascinated by Upton's description of a UU church that embraced diversity and had no fixed set of theological beliefs but instead encourages members and friends to explore, experience, and contemplate all ideas until they arrive at what is personally and spiritually meaningful to them. text: A B cell identifies pathogens when antibodies on its surface bind to a specific foreign antigen. This antigen/antibody complex is taken up by the B cell and processed by proteolysis into peptides. The B cell then displays these antigenic peptides on its surface MHC class II molecules. The surface MHC II molecules, together with T cell recognition of foreign antigens presented in this manner, results in T cell stimulation. T cells are recruited to these sites, stimulate additional B cells to produce antibodies, and thus form a memory to the antigen of interest. These memory B cells remain in the circulatory system, where they are readily recruited during subsequent infections. In the case of infections with a pathogen of specific memory, the cells are quickly activated to form large numbers of antibodies, causing rapid onset of disease. On the other hand, if foreign antigens do not appear, memory cells that may otherwise be recruited to a site remain in the circulatory system. This allows the patient to mount a rapid tissue response at a later time when the antigen surfaces. In this way, antibodies allow a rapid response to specific antigens. The development of memory B cells is central to adaptive immunity. 33 Although this principle is not directly associated with the current discussion of T cell regulation, the discussion is included here to emphasize again the close relationship between humoral and cellular immunity. The development of memory T cells is also central to adaptive immunity.

The Lobata have a pair of lobes, which are muscular, cuplike extensions of the body that project beyond the mouth. Their inconspicuous tentacles originate from the corners of the mouth, running in convoluted grooves and spreading out over the inner surface of the lobes (rather than trailing far behind, as in the Cydippida). The Lobata have 3 or 4 mucus sacs (either two on the tip of the head or two on the back of the head). The two larger mucus sacs seem to be associated with lobe production, or perhaps with lobe swelling. Another mucus gland, smaller than those associated with lobes, is usually situated midway between the two larger mucus glands. The surface area of the mucus glands is 5 to 8
fold that of a copepod. The Lobata have either five or six pairs of short legs. Each leg may contain one spine or hook. The swimming legs resemble miniature copepod legs. When alarmed, the copepod moves rapidly towards the bottom, but instead of burying in the sediment, it hides itself in a sheltered place by making the lobes sink rapidly into the sediment. However, it is sometimes observed resting on the bottom or buried in sediment, the lobes being drawn in and kept up by means of a contractile organ. Many individuals are found hidden in the sediment; those on the bottom of the water column or in deeper sediment may be overlooked (Stimpson 1853).

There have been debates as to whether civil disobedience must necessarily be non-violent. Black's Law Dictionary includes non-violence in its definition of civil disobedience. Christian Bay's encyclopedia article states that civil disobedience requires "carefully chosen and legitimate means," but holds that they do not have to be non-violent. According to the Encyclopedia of the American Civil Rights Movement, Martin Luther King favored civil disobedience, but stated "the choice is his" as to whether the method should be non-violent.

Other views of civil disobedience include Aaron Wildavsky, who held that non-violence and civility as goals are not necessary to qualify an act as civil disobedience. Wildavsky held that nonviolence is only a means of attaining peaceful ends. Furthermore, he held that even where the act is not violent, the civil disobedience does not necessarily have to conform to rules or expectations of a particular government. As of 2012, Wildavsky's views were generally not taken into consideration in the academic discussion of civil disobedience.

Following the Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction event, the extinction of the dinosaurs and the wetter climate may have allowed the tropical rainforest to spread out across the continent. This led to the diversification in the Early Miocene of South American monkeys, cats, dogs and rodents. The earliest known species in these groups lived in the Early Miocene, an era in which they shared the continent with early horses, tapirs and many other terrestrial animals. Modern-looking species began to appear during the Late Miocene, 13 million years ago. One of these was the cat-like jaguar; the early horse, Equus; and the tapir. At the same time, the first primates entered the continent. At the end of the Miocene, the first species of peccary appeared, about 9 million years ago. The modern peccary is a descendent of the early Miocene peccary.

text: Ctenophores form an animal phylum that is more complex than sponges, about as complex as cnidarians (jellyfish, sea anemones, etc. ), and less complex than bilaterians (which include almost all other animals). In other words, they're on the cusp between complex and simple. Their main advantage over sponges is that they have a better circulatory system that allows them to move and also to take in food: at the same time, they also have a nervous system that allows them to respond to changes in the environment while having the same level of complexity and number or cell types as sponges. Ctenophores are also simple enough that they have one gene (in some species) that allows them an anatomical flexibility unknown in sponges. [A more recent paper gives a different date for ctenophores: 495 million years]. In 2008, one of the first complete ctenophore genome was published. It's been pretty exciting to see that they too have a lot of gene duplication. In fact, they have a lot more than sponges (see Figure 10). So they are also an excellent model to study gene duplication (especially in this paper: Kaguni and Wainwright). the thermal fluctuations that exist at very low temperature in disordered systems are often attributed to the existence of some two - level excitations . It is important to point out that the theory of this kind is not applicable to these systems. According to the ideas that exist in the theory of disordered systems, the thermal agitation on the atom-like is due to the hopping or tunnelling of an atom like object ( a two-level excitation ). But, as you say, the thermal agitation on our object is not due to this sort of energy . We therefore must study the thermal agitation on our object from a different point of view . The Victorian Constitution can be amended by the Parliament of Victoria, except for certain "entrenched" provisions that require either an absolute majority in both houses, a three-fifths majority in both houses, or the approval of the Victorian people in a referendum, depending on the provision. Section 83 of the constitution establishes a constitutional monarchy in Victoria under which the governor is appointed by the governor-general but is responsible to the parliament. In the 21st century the Victorian governor is both the state's representative and the head of Victoria's executive government. The governor resides at Government House in Melbourne, and is provided to by the Lieutenant Governor.

Proportionality is recognised one of the general principles of European Union law by the European Court of Justice since the 1950s. According to the general principle of proportionality the lawfulness of an action depends on whether it was appropriate and necessary to achieve the objectives legitimately pursued. When there is a choice between several appropriate measures the least onerous must be adopted, and any disadvantage caused must not be disproportionate to the aims pursued. The European Court of Justice explained the necessity element by declaring in the
2000 case of Van Gend en Loos that a European Community institution was not bound by the rules of international law and thus the EC institutions were endowed the necessary power, in accordance with the rule of proportionality, to change the law. Later they explained that under the principle of proportionality the Community institutions are not entitled to act in circumstances where the action could seriously damage individual rights or individual liberties or lead to serious economic problems. A number of legal rules have been formulated to delimit the principle of proportionality, which include the test of necessity and the test of reasonableness. The principle itself has many facets: it provides protection from illegality by enabling the principle to be invoked when a statutory provision is invalid. In addition, the principle protects from any kind of public power abuse by prohibiting the Member States to enact laws, which they consider urgent to execute but which affect individuals rights and liberties. Above all, the principle of proportionality prevents the governmental actions from being overturned on the grounds that its nature was abnormal. The principle of proportionality is therefore intended to defend rights protected by general principles of law and fundamental values of the community. Advances in polynomial algebra were made by mathematicians during the Yuan era. The mathematician Zhu Shijie (1249–1314) solved simultaneous equations with up to four unknowns using a rectangular array of coefficients, equivalent to modern matrices. He also solved equations with more than four unknowns by using a "little" array and matrices, solving many equations simultaneously. The mathematician Shen Kuo (1225–1296) also studied matrix algebra. Later, the matrix method became popular and played an important role in Chinese mathematics during the Ming and Qing Dynasties (see Wu Wen-Bai below).

### Later developments

In the 17th C, Huang Xuewei solved a sequence of 2-by-2 systems of congruences using a method that included several modern ideas, such as using congruences instead of linear equations, rewriting linear equations into one single congruence and then solving for one unknown at a time using the modern concept of a ratio.

In Europe, François Viète (1540–1603) developed the matrix method for solving systems of linear equations. Viète made a breakthrough in the study of matrices, generalizing concepts such as the determinant, and using ideas from matrix algebra in a geometric setting. His innovations had a major impact on future developments in matrix algebra.

Man with the Screaming Brain certainly isn't a perfect movie, but I'm pretty sure it was never meant to be anything more than a star vehicle for Bruce Campbell, meaning it works as kind of a summary of his entire career: slapstick, sarcasm, cheese, action, and happy endings. Campbell is, as a writer, uneven--there are lots of things in the story that don't make a great deal of sense (why does the robot suddenly have breasts merely because a female brain has been implanted into it? ), and some of the scenes feel like retreads of other, better incarnations (the scene in the restaurant, where Yegor and William battle for control of William's body, is straight out of Evil Dead II). And yet: despite all this, I was engaged throughout the movie, because it is so clearly a labor of love for Bruce Campbell. Even though it is a low budget movie, it is made with skill, and has great production design (the robots, despite their small stature, look pretty badass), and despite the often overly comical tone, there are a few genuine moments of poignancy or emotion. I don't think Man with the Screaming Brain is a classic--I don't think it'll be the sort of movie that I'll watch again the first time I see it--but it makes a nice change of pace, and gives some people a chance to sit back and enjoy Campbell's work, and also enjoy a good alien movie.

Using a system of two equations that together with the churn rate describe both network and flow dynamics, we analytically derive a phase transition threshold in which flow reaches non-zero on the network . By using experimental data acquired from the Tor network, our results on Tor demonstrate that, although the Tor network is self- organizing with relatively small rate of churn , the Tor network shows the existence of flow which keeps non- zero throughout the time . When peer to peer network is operating smoothly with few changes, i.e. low churn rate , this indicates that the Tor flow is kept non- zero by the network dynamics itself. On the other hand, if the churn rate increases, i.e. becomes in- steady state, the system starts to operate unstable with large perturbation. The stability analysis on the Tor overlay network can be used to design an optimized churn rate to maintain stable network and flow states.

there are many treatment modalities available to acutely terminate incessant ventricular tachycardia with variable success rates , but some cases tend to prove refractory to all of them . However , the rate of refilling of the left ventricular ( LV ) cavity is most important, which is achieved through optimal diastolic function .
Ventricular diastolic dysfunction is usually a late consequence of ischaemia and is usually related to a loss of myofibre function and a consequent loss of distensibility , both of which appear after a period of ischaemia and reperfusion but before significant myocardial damage occurs . The impaired ability to relax is accompanied by a decrease in myosin content , presumably due to the lack of energy input and also by a loss of actin content that prevents the reorganization of myofibres and decreases their number , thus reducing their distensibility , in most cases leading to diastolic dysfunction .

text: Following the Nice Treaty, there was an attempt to reform the constitutional law of the European Union and make it more transparent; this would have also produced a single constitutional document. However, as a result of the referendum in France and the referendum in the Netherlands, the 2004 Treaty establishing a Constitution for Europe never came into force. Instead, the Lisbon Treaty was enacted. The key feature of the Lisbon Treaty was the transfer of competence on the part of the intergovernmental European Council to the European Parliament and the European Commission. The main goal of the Lisbon Treaty, as stated in Article 7, was to ensure “the greatest possible” transparency and legality in European legislation. According to Article 2, the European Parliament would become a colegislator on equal terms with the European Council. The Treaties establish the EU's institutions, list their powers and responsibilities, and explain the areas in which the EU can legislate with Directives or Regulations. A fundamental provision of the Treaties is the Community method, by which the EU decides on policies and legislates for implementation throughout its member states. The treaties (and in particular the TEU) provide the legal foundation on which the EU operates. While all member states are subject to the law of the EU and to the jurisdiction of theCourt of Justice of the European Union, the EU itself cannot take a legal action except through its national member states. The principle of cooperation has become the "foundation" of the EU political system and has enabled the European Commission to develop a significant degree of coordination of national policies without imposing decisions. With cooperating member states and an independent judiciary, the EU can address complex issues without imposing its decisions. Director Don Siegel really impressed me with this film. It is starkly shot, graphic without being visually graphic, well-acted by all concerned, and covers some of the most taboo issues of any day in a workmanlike, almost expected normalcy hitherto not seen in any other film by this reviewer. I didn't know what to expect sitting down to watch this: a civil war movie or some kind of 70's soft-core peddling with Eastwood descending on a school for girls in the South. Well, the latter is closer than you might imagine, but it is a bit more than that. Eastwood puts in a very real, almost humanized performance as Schofield, a man whose morals are somewhat questionable, and yet he seems the only moral person in a story where almost everyone else is selling their souls for little money. That said, I was a bit let down by the ending which seemed like any other film of that genre. It was an amusing tale told of the most interesting things that can happen when a war breaks out between two groups of people, and where everyone seems to lose in the end, yet everyone gains some kind of satisfaction regardless. One of the better made films of its type. I can't recommend this enough.

text: In many poor and developing countries much land and housing is held outside the formal or legal property ownership registration system. The land and housing are usually registered informally with local officials or with a local authority but there is no formal public registration system in many countries. This results in the land or housing being considered as "unowned" or "unowned" in the official property registration system, which may mean that there is no official record that they exist. Even if the land or housing is registered by a local official, for example in a community or traditional area, this registration is not recognized by the national property registration system. According to the UN-Habitat definition of informal settlements, some types of legal land and housing ownership systems include informal settlements or "unauthorized settlements". However, only the land and housing belonging to "unowned" or "unowned" (in the official national property registration system) is typically part of such informal settlements (i.e. such areas are occupied in violation of relevant laws or without permission or prior to property registration and such areas are occupied by people to live in). It is important to note that some types of informal settlements may have land or housing ownership rights that are formal (i.e. recorded in a national property register). It is also important to note that informal settlements usually fall into categories (e.g. squatter settlements), which may (or may not) exist in other countries with different legal land and housing ownership regimes and different types of informal settlements. Both X.25 and Frame Relay provide connection-oriented operations. But X.25 does it at the network layer of the OSI Model. Frame Relay does it at level two, the data link layer.
Both X.25 and Frame Relay provide connectionless networks, which can send messages from node to node without establishing a dedicated connection before sending packets. These connectionless networks are not as reliable as connection-oriented networks, though; Frame Relay can only guarantee delivery of about 99.5% of a message. Since X.25 is at the network layer, its connectionless capability can guarantee 100% delivery; however, this guarantees delivery at the cost of connection setup times. In addition to X.25's and Frame Relay's ability to connect to an IBM mainframe via serial connection at 1.54 Mbps, the networks can send messages to each other at the same speed. text: Several barriers protect organisms from infection, including mechanical, chemical, and biological barriers. The waxy cuticle of many leaves, the exoskeleton of insects, the shells and membranes of externally deposited eggs, and skin are examples of mechanical barriers that are the first line of defense against infection. However, as organisms cannot be completely sealed from their environments, other systems act to protect body openings such as the lungs, intestines, and the genitourinary tract. Chemical barriers are produced by glands on or beneath the skin and include hydrocarbons that cover body hair. These chemicals may repel pathogens and parasites. Biological barriers include the mucous coating that lines the esophagus, the lymph system, and the phagocytic cells in the blood and lymph systems. These cell systems use their receptor systems to distinguish between cell and pathogen surfaces. Once identified as the target for the virus, these cells undergo an intracellular signaling transduction process that culminates in the pathogen becoming food for the phagocytic cell. Once absorbed, this material is either destroyed or excreted. A number of pathogenic viruses, bacteria, and protozoans have been identified that subvert or bypass some barriers. Once inside a host organism, a virus, bacteria, or protozoa can disrupt or interfere with processes that function to control or regain homeostasis. In 1928, he married actress and dancer Martha Bongo, also of the ""Broadway Boom"" of 1921. Some sources even say Johnny was homosexual.

She was a total, absolute, no-exceptions star - and not just because of her unique beauty, but because she was able to project great emotions into her work. And in a very complex stage role, no less. text: Decision problems are one of the central objects of study in computational complexity theory. A decision problem is a special type of computational problem whose answer is either yes or no, or alternately either 1 or 0. A decision problem can be viewed as a formal language, where the members of the language are instances whose output is yes, and the non-members are those instances whose output is no. The question of interest is: on what inputs will the problem accept yes? The difficulty of this question is measured with a complexity measure often called the decision complexity. Decision complexity is central in the complexity theory of many-one reductions, the computational theory of random generators, the problem of non-determinism (the Turing problem), and as of late, the study of circuit complexity. The Turing problem is, on our view, the most fundamental problem in computational complexity theory. The Turing problem is (roughly) to answer whether given a circuit, the output will be yes. One of the key results of decision complexity theory is circuit-decision completeness. Specifically, there exist polynomial time reductions from the decision version of circuit complexity to both the decision version of the Turing problem and to the decision version of random generation. text: Hypersensitivity is an immune response that damages the body's own tissues. They are divided into four classes (Type I – IV) based on the mechanisms involved and the time course of the hypersensitive reaction. Type I hypersensitivity is an immediate or anaphylactic reaction, often associated with allergy. The most common Type I allergies are allergy to food and reactions to vaccines. Type II hypersensitivity is also called cytotoxic or cell-mediated hypersensitivity. In this type of hypersensitivity, antibodies or T-cells attack the cell or organism (often a virus), thereby eliminating the target. The response is specific, requires the target to be present, and does not occur until the target appears. Type III (or mixed) hypersensitivity is a mixed response consisting of both Type I and II reactions. In such a case, the immediate hypersensitivity reaction that often occurs is followed by an anti-body response that, in turn, causes an immunological challenge to the organism or cell. It is this response that can lead to an autoimmune disease. Type IV hypersensitive does not involve a cell-mediated response, since only antibodies are involved. Complexity Approach This approach seeks to understand the inherent limits imposed by the way the machine operates. In general, a computation requires both time and space. Time, measured by the length of a sequence of instructions which are executed one after the other by the computer s machine language, can be thought of as the basic unit of computing. It is a fundamental property which must be measured and for which algorithms must be developed. Time is often expressed in terms of the number of ticks on the computer s clock, but other units, such as the number of instructions, the number of bits moved, or the number of bytes of disk storage used are also used. Spatial complexity, or the amount of storage space used in the machine s data structure, is also an important factor. The system of bureaucracy created by Kublai Khan reflected various cultures in the empire, including that of the Han Chinese, Khitans, Jurchens, Mongols, and Tibetan Buddhists. While the official terminology of the institutions may indicate the government structure was almost purely that of native Chinese dynasties, the Yuan bureaucracy actually consisted of a mix of elements from different cultures. The Chinese-style elements of the bureaucracy mainly came from the native Tang, Song, as well as Khitan Liao and Jurchen Jin dynasties. Other elements came from the Yuan-Mongolian dynasty, such as the use of the title Zao (Mongolian) to refer to the highest executive institution, the Khutukhian (Jurchen) system of the division of labor established by Genghis Khan for the military in campaigns, and the division of labor in the Yao, Yi, and Li, an institution for the management of labor used during the Yuan Dynasty. The Yuan had also previously introduced a system of land taxation, which had not been employed by the Song, only beginning to be adopted and developed by the Ming dynasties. In the Yuan bureaucracy, this land tax system was modified and combined with the Chinese government's collectors of grain and other taxes, eventually resulting in the development of Chinese-style centralized taxation.

text: The Normans had a profound effect on Irish culture and history after their invasion at Bannow Bay in 1169. They brought with them the feudal system, which had been the basis of European power for the past five hundred years. As a result, the land and the people alike became the property of the overlords the Normans, whose authority was backed up by the institution of 'patrimonial' heritage, namely a system whereby the family members were obliged to follow the example of the ancestors. Because this 'ancestral' system had a major impact on social life and on the development of the Irish language, it has come to be regarded as one of the most important aspects of the Norman influence. The Normans introduced the feudal system because that method had been effective in the past and the Normans believed that only that method could ensure a lasting social order. Social life before the Norman invasions was based on the tribal system. The tribe was the primary unit of society, with the extended family being the second. The tentacles of cydippid ctenophores are typically fringed with tentilla ("little tentacles"), although a few genera have simple tentacles without these sidebranches. The tentacles and tentilla are densely covered with microscopic colloblasts that capture prey by sticking to it. Colloblasts are specialized mushroom-shaped cells in the outer layer of the epidermis, and have three main components: a domed head with vesicles (chambers) that contain adhesive; a stalk that anchors the cell in the lower layer of the epidermis or in the mesoglea; and a spiral thread that coils round the stalk and is attached to the head and to the root of the stalk. The colloblasts are specialized to exert a strong adhesive force when triggered by touch.
Colloblasts have two main forms: mushroom-shaped (cap) cells with a single stalk and spherical cells with three stalk segments. The spherical cells are more common in species that hug objects such as bacterium-coated rods and algae. Their mushroom-shaped counterparts are more prevalent in species that hunt by scanning the surrounding sea water for small particles of organic matter, and then suck these particles into their tentacles. In either case, the spherical cells are predominant in the tentacle tips, and in species that hunt by scanning the surrounding sea water their mushroom-shaped counterparts are prevalent in the tentacle bases. Both forms are predominant in species that hunt by scanning the sea floor (including species that hunt for other small animals in this way). In these species, a significant proportion of the colloblasts are mushroom shaped, but it is as yet unclear why this is.

The name Rijn, from here on, is used only for smaller streams farther to the north, which together formed the main river Rhine in Roman times. Though they retained the name, these streams no longer carry water from the Rhine, but are used for draining the surrounding land and polders. From Wijk bij Duurstede, the old north branch of the Rhine is called Kromme Rijn ("Bent Rhine") past Utrecht, first Leidse Rijn ("Rhine of Leiden") and then, Oude Rijn ("Old Rhine").

### Landscape

Around Wijk bij Duurstede, the river is marked by several dykes. Between these dykes the Krimpense laagten (Krimpense Lowlands) were created.

The Dutch Rhine has many islands such as Stellingwerfs Eiland (Island Stellingwerf).

Near Dordrecht the river is crossed by the former railway tunnel Oude Maas – Hollandsche Ijzeren Spoorweg – Spoorweg Maassluis – Spoorlijn 127 – Stationsweg which was replaced by the bridge N206.

### Navigation

This motivates the concept of a problem being hard for a complexity class. A problem X is hard for a class of problems C if every problem in C can be reduced to X. Thus no problem in C is harder than X, since an algorithm for X allows us to solve any problem in C. Of course, the notion of hard problems depends on the type of reduction being used. It is easy to show that such a notion is not well-defined for P. Easy problems are those, for which every problem in C can be reduced to X. But for any NP problem there will exist an algorithm that solves that problem and many others in NP. Thus NP is hard for P, since the algorithm will imply a reduction from many NP problems. The reduction will be of a form that takes any NP problem and transforms it into the problem whose answer we know. We will assume that knowing its solution implies knowing the solution of at least the many NP problems. text: Space Without Eyes"To localize an object means simply to represent the movements that would be necessary to reach it." These words of the great French mathematician and physicist Henri Poincaré offer a bold statement of an idea that goes back to George Berkeley: the experience of space is grounded, finally, in our sense of our bodies, in our sense of our own degrees of freedom of movement.Berkeley thought that touch was the spatial sense, for it was the movement sense. Vision without touch would deliver only flat pictures of the world around us.But what about touch without vision? The sense of pressure, in particular of touch, is a powerful grounding for experience of space. It delivers vivid, rich, and multidimensional spatial experience, for us on our own bodies, but also, with our hands and bodies, when we move in spaces we can see, through seeing or touching or both. It is a highly local, highly situational activity that grounds all spatial experience without being visible to our eyes.This book, by Alan H. Dougherty, presents a powerful and highly original investigation of the sense of touch that grounds our experience of space. In Touch explains how we come to feel the pressure of our bodies on the ground, how our sense of touch grows with our own freedom to move about, and how our understanding of touch is intimately interwoven with an understanding of space.

Then a simple criterion of having one-third of contacts established is usually used . Here we present a few alternative ways of looking at the problem by examining the effects of having a fraction of contacts established and also varying the time spent by the protein in the native state .
Making contact requires some amount of relative motion. Relative motion can often be described by the mean square displacement of a protein which is proportional to time with a characteristic relaxation time. The exponential growth of the mean squared displacements with time is usually called the stretched exponential model. For proteins that are undergoing contact formation with two other molecules, the mean square displacement of the protein gives us the time that the contacting molecules remain in contact and does not need to be differentiated with time. This was studied previously and the distribution of contact lengths in the time during which the contacts are being formed is derived . Then we use an average length of contacts for various time periods to relate the time spent by a protein undergoing contact formation with a fraction of contacts that are established at that time.

There were Huguenots in Ireland from the late 16th century onwards, especially since the end of Kinsale. They continued to emigrate to Ireland from France in the 17th century. The conquest of Cyprus by the Anglo-Norman forces of the Third Crusade opened a new chapter in the history of the island, which would be under Western European domination for the following 380 years. Although not part of a planned operation, the conquest had much more permanent results than initially expected. The island would become a centre of European trade, which the Greeks would for centuries try to curb.
The island’s size and the fact that it was a colony of the Roman Empire made it useful as a base for the Roman Navy in antiquity. From the time of the Third Crusade, Cyprus would become an important Mediterranean colony of the European medieval states. In particular Venice played a key role in its colonisation because, thanks to its access to the Black Sea, it would make Cyprus the central island in its system of maritime trade empire, which had expanded in the Middle Ages.
As with other places, the presence of Western Europeans and their settlement was accompanied by the construction of churches.
The construction of many churches in the 12th and 13th centuries was related to the settlement of the island. text: Free oxygen gas was almost nonexistent in Earth's atmosphere before photosynthetic archaea and bacteria evolved, probably about 3.5 billion years ago. Free oxygen first appeared in significant quantities during the Paleoproterozoic eon (between 3.0 and 2.3 billion years ago). Paleoterrestrial and aerobic archaea, such as Methanococcoides, might have contributed to oxygen release. Ancillary factors such as the growth of oxygen-using bacteria (such as cyanobacteria) also contributed to the rise of free oxygen. Photosynthetic cyanobacteria may have been the most significant phototrophic group in the evolutionary history of free oxygen. Oxygen and water were released by early photosynthetic organisms, providing an environment in which other organisms could develop. These other organisms included some of the earliest free-living organisms capable of using oxygen as an electron acceptor for ATP generation. Atmospheric oxygen rose sharply around the time that free oxygen-using bacteria appeared (such as those used in chemo-synthesis and bio-synthesis to make metabolic products), and reached about 20% O2 by the mid-Cambrian period. In the atmosphere, oxygen reacts with many other elements to form compounds that are not normally found on Earth's surface: oxides of nitrogen (NOx), sulfur (SOx), and carbon (COx) are all common in the atmosphere caused by the oxygen released by photosynthesis. The atmosphere today contains a higher concentration of oxidizing power (ozone) than ever before in Earth's history and is much more unstable than before when life evolved.

text:
The Rhine was not known to Herodotus and first enters the historical period in the 1st century BC in Roman-era geography. At that time, it formed the boundary between Gaul and Germania. The Upper Rhine had been part of the areal of the late Hallstatt culture since the 6th century BC, and by the 1st century BC, the areal of the La Tène culture covered almost its entire length, forming a contact zone with the Jastorf culture, i.e. a border zone of Germanic settlement between the lower Rhine basin and the northern Alpine regions.
The Roman writer Tacitus recorded some accounts about the upper Rhine, based on their settlement patterns. The higher Rhine valleys, including the High Alps, lay north of the territory of the Helvetii who are named in the Commentarii de Bello Gallico. The Helvetii are recorded as having occupied the Rhine-to-Aare corridor; the Roman historian and geographer Strabo is not as clearly recorded as Tacitus. However, he wrote about the upper Rhine valley during his own times, which implies that Roman records existed already during his time and probably the upper Rhine region was also inhabited by Celts in the early Roman period.
The Rhine had been part of the Germanic sphere since the 1st century BC and became part of the Roman Empire in the 1st century AD, when the Germanic tribes were settled as Roman allies. Rome controlled the Rhine until 368, and since the early 3rd century, the Romans also built many fortification along the Rhine from Basel at the northwest to Mainz at the southwest. The strong Rhine was a natural fortification which required a large number of ships along the river—in total over 3.000 ships—to be built and transported along the river.

text: Many machine models different from the standard multi-tape Turing machines have been proposed in the literature, for example random access machines. Perhaps surprisingly, each of these models can be converted to another without providing any extra computational power. We discuss this in detail in Section 2.5. In fact, the standard tape Turing machines are capable of emulating just about every known machine model. This is because standard tape Turing machines can compute an infinite number of strings. This can be used to compute the output of random access machines (which do not have an infinite tape). Similarly, random access machines can emulate standard tape Turing machines (and then emulate standard tape machines). We discuss this in more detail in Section 5.8.

Due to its electronegativity, oxygen forms chemical bonds with almost all other elements to give corresponding oxides. The surface of most metals, such as aluminium and titanium, are oxidized in the presence of air and become coated with a thin film of oxide that passivates the metal and slows further corrosion.
These metal oxides are also used as catalysts for certain reactions to speed up a chemical reaction. The simplest metal oxide, magnesium oxide, is an ionic oxide with a layer of negatively charged oxygen ions held together by negatively charged magnesium ions. The metal oxides can be classified by the type of bonding by the relative electro negativity of silicon dioxide has the lowest ionic bonding, while the compounds of the highest electro negativity (platinum groups of elements) are metallic monoxides.

text: On August 15, 1971, the United States unilaterally pulled out of the Bretton Woods Accord. The US abandoned the Gold Exchange Standard whereby the value of the dollar had been pegged to the price of gold and all other currencies were pegged to the dollar, whose value was left to "float" (rise and fall according to market demand). Shortly thereafter, Britain followed, floating the pound sterling. The US dollar plummeted as demand for gold increased, while Britain's pound sterling rose. On August 16, 1971, President Nixon announced that the US was unilaterally "going off the gold standard." He said the United States' "excessive gold purchases" by foreign central banks had "depleted" the government's gold reserves to such an extent that "there can be little doubt that the excess purchases have seriously affected the US dollar position." The success of any pathogen depends on its ability to elude host immune responses. Therefore, pathogens evolved several methods that allow them to successfully infect a host, while evading detection or destruction by the immune system. Such pathogens are highly successful, leading to a constant threat of disease outbreaks. Therefore, it is important to understand the mechanisms of immune evasion. The shape of the ciliated animals' body (the so-called rhizoplume) has been shown to affect ciliary beating speed and therefore has affected locomotion. Ctenophores, like all ciliated animals, have two rows of cilia on the back of the rhizoplume that, if the animal is large enough, beat synchronously. This has been shown to cause a "swimming" motion of the rhizoplume, allowing ctenophores of sufficient size to swim faster than the surrounding water through what is known as the "stirring effect." text: Problems that can be solved in theory (e.g., given large but finite time), but which in practice take too long for their solutions to be useful, are known as intractable problems. In complexity theory, problems that lack polynomial-time solutions are considered to be intractable for more than the smallest inputs. In fact, the Cobham–Edmonds thesis states that only those problems that can be solved in polynomial time can be feasibly computed on some computational device. Examples of intractable problems include the travelling salesman problem, the knapsack problem and graph isomorphism. Note that finding a way to solve a problem efficiently is not necessarily a feasible task. That is to say, some of the following tasks may be intractable by themselves, even if they are not intractable in general. An example is finding an efficient way to compute the inverse of some matrix, a problem that is considered in linear algebra when finding a solution to a system of linear equations. Given some time, an efficient algorithm can be identified that will solve the problem in time O(n), where n is the size of the matrix. When this matrix is the adjacency matrix of the graph, the problem of finding the inverse of the corresponding matrix is known as the graph inversion problem. However, it is known that a linear algebra algorithm must run in time O(n2), and the complexity of the problem is therefore intractable. In an attempt to reduce the time required to compute solutions to intractable problems, a number of techniques have been developed.

Visconti paints the atmosphere of this lost world so hauntingly that you might find yourself wishing to turn back time and never have left this lush, beautiful place. Waco: The Rules of Engagement dissects the evidence behind the standoff in Waco, Texas that led to the destruction of the Branch Davidian homestead and the alleged government cover-up.

The first thing you need to know about this film: you will see brief but disturbing photos of the victims bodies. This is not done for shock value, but to illustrate points about the way they died, as if you were present at the coroner's inquest.

The second thing you should know about this film: at two and a quarter hours, it's pretty ponderous - especially if you already followed the events closely at the time. If you are unaware of any of the events other than what was reported in the mass media, or if the only side of the story you are familiar with is the official government report, this may be essential viewing. But for most of you, there may be something less taxing to watch.

Waco's true story is about more than mere history - about things that have happened before, and may happen again. It's about the abuse of power, and the loss of individual rights. It's about the government of the United States and the "weapon" of "prevention".

It's about the things that went wrong in this tragedy, and the things that didn't go right. It's about the government attempting to cover-up an embarrassing debacle, and about how the media has responded to this event after the fact. But most of all, it's about truth, and being able to discern it from the lies. This is not the full story, but it is one piece of a more complete picture. Funding for private schools is generally provided through student tuition, endowments, scholarship/voucher funds, and donations and grants from religious organizations or private individuals. Government funding for religious schools is either subject to restrictions or possibly forbidden, according to the courts' interpretation of the Establishment Clause of the First Amendment or individual state Blaine Amendments. Non-religious private schools theoretically could qualify for such funding without hassle, preferring the advantages of independent control of their student admissions and course content instead of the public funding they could get with charter status.
As for public university status, some states allow religious private colleges and universities to confer religious affiliated degrees even though they are private and nonprofit. Others limit degrees to only religious degrees (e.g., theology or biblical studies) even though the school can award degrees in "secular" fields as well. Some states' laws allow religious schools to award degrees in religious subjects but not to offer nonreligious "secular" degree programs. It should be noted that a religious school can confer degrees even though its accreditation does not come from a state agency--although this often increases the difficulty (and sometimes the extra expense) in finding work on one's degree.
One should note that most of the "degree mills" that exist are nonreligious schools that are located in the U.S.--they usually are not legitimate accredited institutions.
For the purpose of the law, private schools in general are simply privately owned companies that sell products and services--including education. They are not different, except legally, than any of the other privately owned schools that also sell education products and services (public schools, privately owned schools).

Chemical kinetic analysis of the nonstatistical vibrational energy relaxation in the planar carbonyl sulfide molecule
Carles CARMENA MUNOZ, Juan Maria VARALO, Enrique RAMOS, Jose Luis DE MARCHI, Raul ROTO, Rafael LUQUEZ
Journal: Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A, Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences / Volume 453 / Issue 1899 / December 1997
The relaxation processes of the non-statistical vibrational energy in the planar carbonyl sulfide molecule are studied from the point of view of chemical kinetic theory. Several experiments indicate that the relaxation process consists of a sequence of abrupt transitions between localized energy regions. The chemical kinetics equations are analytically derived from the equations of motion for the atomic degrees of freedom. The first order chemical reactions between the vibrational excitation and the translation motions include the transitions between the localized vibrational energy regions. Moreover, the non-statistical vibrational energy relaxation time predicted from the chemical equations differs from the statistical one in the sense that the relaxation time is much longer than the statistical time and that the energy does not flow in a statistical manner. Finally, the chemical kinetic equations are compared with the experimental data and satisfactory results are obtained.

text: There are three major types of rock: igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic. The rock cycle is an important concept in geology which illustrates the relationships between these three types of rock, and magma. When a rock crystallizes from melt (magma and/or lava), it is an igneous rock. When a rock is eroded and shatters into smaller particles, it becomes sedimentary. If the sedimentary rock is buried deep under new layers of sediment, it can change into metamorphic rock. Rocks and minerals are used for many different types of products like jewelry or gemstones, to make paint or glass, or to make building products and cement. Rock is also used to help make our electricity. We can split rocks in the ground to help make our electricity, or we can make electricity by running water through rocks. Rock is used to make building blocks, too. When we want to build a school or a house, we use materials like shale, limestone, marble, or granite to make the buildings. These buildings have lots of rocks in them, too. So, when you think about some of the things you have in your house, you might notice that they are made out of rocks and minerals! Educator[edit]
Main article: School pharmacists
School pharmacists are pharmacists that work in schools and provide health-related services to schools and its staff within the United States, and can either take an active role in the life of a school and school community, or an observer role. School pharmacists observe the health-related issues affecting school communities and work with students, parents, faculty, school nurses and administrators to create a healthy school environment that enhances and supports academic achievement.[59]
Pharmaceutical technician[edit]
Technicians in pharmaceutical industries (pharma technicians), do the work related to the development of drugs and the delivery of these drugs to patients and they are responsible for keeping drugs on the market up-to-date and ensuring their quality and efficacy. This involves monitoring and testing to ensure that the product complies with certain regulatory and safety standards, including a variety of quality control steps designed to ensure that the product works as well as it was supposed to, and that it is safe for people to use.[44]
Teaching pharmacist[edit]
Main article: Teaching pharmacist
Teaching pharmacists are pharmacists that work in academic institution and provide health-related services to students and other institution staff within the institution. A teaching pharmacist also can work outside their institution to provide health education services to the public.[60]

text: The history of the steam engine stretches back as far as the first century AD; the first recorded rudimentary steam engine being the aeolipile described by Greek mathematician Hero of Alexandria. In the following centuries, the few steam-powered "engines" known were, like the aeolipile, essentially experimental devices used by inventors to demonstrate the properties of steam. One of the first applications of steam-power to industry was James Watt's patented improvement on the Newcomen engine in the late 18th century. Newcomen had a cylinder surrounded by, rather than in, a container, so that water could be continually replenished in the cylinder. Watt employed a piston that was surrounded by a container, rather than the cylinder being in the container, and also employed a steam valve to regulate the rate of steam injection into the cylinder. The invention of the stationary engine meant that it was no longer necessary to move any part of the engine to utilize the steam energy generated. A major component is the steam generator that heats water to create steam that then powers the crane. Steam generators may be fueled with either natural gas or liquid gas. On liquid fuel steam generators, the liquid fuel, such as kerosene or diesel, mixes with air or natural gas to create a fuel-air mixture that is then injected into the steam generator. A second type of steam generator, the gas-fired steam generator, works in a similar manner, except the fuel is natural gas rather than liquid gas. When natural gas is used as a fuel, it must be processed to remove contaminants such as carbon dioxide, water vapor and hydrogen sulfide. Natural gas-fired steam generators can be found in several applications such as natural gas-fired boiler stations, natural gas-fired gas turbine combined cycle systems and natural gas-fired water tube boilers

The fraction 1/p expressed likewise in base q (rather than base 10) has similar effect, provided that p is not a prime factor of q. Wilson's theorem says that an integer p > 1 is prime if and only if the factorial (p − 1)! = (1/p) has exactly p − 1 distinct prime factors, including 1.

Wilson's theorem can also be applied to irrational numbers. There is a prime between any two consecutive rational multiples (powers) of two non-trivial real numbers x and y; i.e., there is a prime between x/2 and (x/2)² or y/2 and (y/2)². Therefore, there are, for example, no 35-sided primes.

He argues that the media has become a tool for the elite to “manufacture consent” rather than act as an honest means of reporting the truth. His argument is well-rehearsed as a student, but when applied to one of the world’s largest media platforms, it’s easy to see those fears borne out on screen. Fox’s news division is not the least bit shy about embracing its Trump-like character. This is true of the news broadcasts depicted in the film (who seem to rely more on sensational headlines to drive ratings than actual investigative journalism), but also in the way they treat the world at large. For instance, there are numerous calls for violence against certain people and groups. Yet none of these calls seem to lead to any type of actual response. The film actually ends with a news broadcast which shows the media covering the same story three different ways, thus creating a dizzying experience for the audience.
While I don’t think this is a film that would resonate with everyone, I feel strongly that those interested in the world today and how it’s getting to where it is today should definitely consider giving The Day of the Jackal a try. You may be surprised by what you find on screen.

spontaneous spinal epidural hematoma ( sseh ) has been reported as a rare cause of spinal cord compression , especially in children . The reported incidence is 1 in 100000 in the general population and about 1 in 5000 to 3 in children , mainly in the young .
The exact embryological cause of sseh remains unclear. Hypotheses include compression between the dural and an intraspinal vein by the superior articular process during the lumbar-sacral development . As to the spontaneous occurrence of sseh, the only accepted theory is the development of a fragile vein in the lumbosacral dural space without an adequate source for venous drainage . It is known that there are various intracranial, extracranial and spinal vessels in the lumbar and sacral vertebra including the anterior and posterior spinal arteries and vein . It is likely that the intracranial or extracranial artery may supply a small vessel in the subarachnoid space, as the origin of the vessel in the dural sinus. This theory is consistent with the observation of many cases in which the vessels from the upper lumbar artery or the abdominal aorta (the most frequent source of origin of intracranial artery) are identified as the sources of the vein with cavernoma formation or rupture . The diagnosis of aortic rupture remains challenging as no single test is an absolute diagnostic modality. Therefore, a detailed patient history and physical exam by a clinician experienced in treating blunt torso trauma patients can determine the most appropriate diagnostic studies . Our patient's prognosis improved with early surgical exploration and repair of the aortic rupture. Early surgical exploration of vascular injuries also decreases the morbidity of patients with such injuries . In the past, surgical exploration was mandatory for aortic rupture because mortality was greater than 75% . However, with advances in surgical techniques and with the development of less invasive, minimally invasive, and endovascular approaches to the treatment of aortic injuries, the mortality rate for the surgical closure of aortic rupture is now approximately 10% . Surgical repair of aortic rupture is the therapeutic goal of these aortic injured patients . Surgery allows direct access to the aorta and surrounding structures, which can be accessed more easily without an anterior approach.
